docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: This document describes how Agentstakk components fit together. For conventions on authoring skills, profiles, and agents, see AGENTS.md.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: A release contains kk/, the canonical Claude plugin (klaude-plugin/), the generated Codex skills plugin (kodex-plugin/) and the separate Codex guard (kodex-guard/). The root install.sh bootstraps the release. Maintainer tools and fixtures stay in the checkout. The full legacy template lives at v0.26.0-rc.4.

docs.title: Machine delivery
docs.text:
The installer writes immutable release directories under $KK_HOME/releases/ and publishes the stable ~/.local/bin/kk link to $KK_HOME/bin/kk. kk/lib/payload.py stages the declared payload, and validation.py exercises the dispatchers and registered guard adapters. Activation registers user-scope plugins through the local vendor marketplaces and publishes owned Codex files. The journal in state.json records candidate progress, release identities, tool readiness and the rollback target. A single writer lock covers upgrade, rollback, apply and migration.

Claude loads the released plugin directory in place. Codex caches plugins by version. Its skills and guard have separate identities so an ordinary skills release can reuse the reviewed guard. kk/baseline/ contains launcher defaults, generated agents and the generated native policy projections. kk apply validates and writes the owned Codex files from current overrides. Git-marketplace plugin-only installs remain independently managed by the vendors.

Rollback uses the code in the target release. Upgrade prints a recovery command that works even when the active dispatcher is broken. Pruning retains the active release, the rollback target, a pending candidate and recently superseded releases needed by open sessions. The supported window after supersession is 14 days.

docs.title: Retirement script maintenance
docs.text:
kk/lib/migrate.py pins the retirement script and its sibling semver-compare.sh to the same tag. After retirement:

  1. Branch from the retirement tag so the script, helper and template still match. Apply the migration fix and run bash test/test-template-sync.sh on that branch.
  2. Publish just a maintenance Git tag on the tested commit, for example v0.26.0+retirement.1. The migration downloader reads Git tags directly. The suffix keeps the tag outside the numeric stable-tag filter that moves the documentation’s latest alias. Leave GitHub’s latest release pointing to the current machine release. The normal stable release workflow publishes from master and is for releasing kk itself.
  3. On the normal release line, move RETIREMENT_VERSION to that maintenance tag for the next kk release. Until then adopters can select the patch with kk migrate --retirement-version TAG.

Keep the default branch’s compatibility script in place for old sync clients. RC4 is the retirement tag used by the first cleaned-up release. ADR 0014

docs.title: kk Plugin (klaude-plugin/)
docs.text:
The canonical source of truth for all workflow functionality. Contains:

  • skills/ — 16 workflow and utility skills (/kk:design, /kk:implement, /kk:review-code, /kk:test, /kk:document, /kk:clarify-docs, /kk:handoff, etc.)
  • commands/ — Slash commands for isolated/variant invocations
  • agents/ — Sub-agent definitions (code-reviewer, design-reviewer, spec-reviewer, architecture-reviewer, eval-grader, profile-resolver)
  • profiles/ — Per-domain content (Go, Java, JS/TS, Kotlin, K8s, Python) with detection rules, review checklists, implementation gotchas, design prompts, test validators, and doc rubrics
  • hooks/ — Session instructions and plugin-root export at SessionStart, permission guard at PreToolUse
  • instructions/ — Behavioral instructions and the Git-marketplace plugin-root guidance
  • statusline/ — Basic and enhanced Claude statusline scripts
  • scripts/ — Plugin-root resolver and canonical guard/ wrapper, Python engine, policy declaration and license

Skills reference shared instructions via symlinks to skills/_shared/. Profiles are referenced via ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/profiles/ paths (substituted at plugin-load time by the Claude Code harness).

/kk:handoff is an explicitly invoked, instructions-only utility that publishes active-task context and a starter prompt to a new secret GitHub gist using gh. It has no runtime helper, lifecycle hook or indexing dependency. Its nested agents/openai.yaml is Codex invocation metadata copied unchanged by generation, not a sub-agent definition. Both hosts disable implicit invocation. The CLI stub under its evals/ directory is offline test support only.

docs.title: Profile Vendoring (cmd/vendor-profiles/)
docs.text:
scripts/go-vendor-manifest.yml pins upstream Go guidance and maps it into profile phases. Run make vendor-profiles, then make generate-kodex to refresh both plugin variants. Fix transformations in the generator; direct edits to vendored output are overwritten on the next refresh.

The generator rewrites relative Markdown links to files vendored into the same phase and preserves external URLs. For prose navigation such as See `samber/cc-skills-golang@golang-naming` skill, it prefers a same-phase target, then links to a copy in another packaged phase using ../<phase>/<file>. If several other phases contain the source, the lexically first phase/file path wins, independent of manifest order.

A parenthesized filename such as (testing.md) after a skill reference selects that skill's references/testing.md. It links only when that specific file is packaged; it does not fall back to the broader skill overview.

When a prose reference has no packaged target, its descriptive text survives as plain Related topics: guidance. For example, a reference to an unvendored safety skill still retains “nil interface trap and nil error comparison pitfalls.” Only navigation without descriptive text is removed. Mixed reference lists retain available targets and their surrounding description; fenced examples remain unchanged. Index descriptions use plain-text link labels before truncation, so previews cannot introduce broken links or extra checklist-loading edges.

docs.title: Codex Generation (cmd/generate-kodex/)
docs.text:
A Go tool that transforms klaude-plugin/ into Codex-compatible artifacts:

  • kodex-plugin/ — Skills with ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} and ${TOOLBOX_PLUGIN_ROOT} resolved to relative paths, installed-path root-resolution instructions, injected headers, and copied profiles
  • kk/baseline/codex/agents/*.toml — Sub-agent markdown converted to TOML with developer_instructions for the machine release

Driven by scripts/kodex-generate-manifest.yml. Run via make generate-kodex.

Codex resolves the plugin root from the installed skill's absolute SKILL.md path: the root is the parent of skills/. Generated relative paths such as ../../profiles/ are relative to the installed skill directory, not the consumer's working directory. The generator rewrites Claude-specific shell lookup instructions; Codex does not look up TOOLBOX_PLUGIN_ROOT. When delegating, the parent supplies the absolute root under ## Plugin Root and expands checklist paths before passing them. Sub-agents report a missing root instead of discovering one themselves. Profile authoring checklists retain literal Claude variable names because they describe the canonical Claude plugin's conventions.

Agent generation also translates the canonical frontmatter tools list into a Codex Tool Access section. Read, Grep, and Glob permit their native Codex equivalents, including read-only exec_command calls when dedicated file tools are unavailable. Tool wrappers such as functions.exec carry those calls without granting additional operations. Capy search is included only for agents that declare it. The eval grader keeps only file reading and its fixture-access prohibition; the profile resolver keeps its worktree/plugin path restriction. Unknown tool declarations fail generation instead of being silently discarded. An explicit empty list permits no tool operations; an omitted list keeps the source's inherited-access behavior.

These operation restrictions are instructions, not a separate Codex runtime tool allowlist. Generated agents retain sandbox_mode = "read-only" and explicitly prohibit edits, test/script execution, and permission escalation. This follows the Codex custom-agent configuration model. The read_only_tool_guidance transform removes contradictory Claude-only tool claims from generated agents and runtime-read skill procedures. Canonical Claude files and profile authoring guidance retain their provider-specific conventions.

docs.title: Permission Guard
docs.text:
klaude-plugin/scripts/guard/guard-rules.json declares secrets globs, destructive categories, temporary roots and protected configuration paths. The plugin's guard.sh invokes run-guard.py with isolated Python and checks its output; failures deny. The launcher imports the adjacent guard.py by absolute path, permitting Python's normal bytecode cache without adding project directories to the import search path. The standalone Codex adapters pass --no-bytecode to the wrapper so running a hook leaves its reviewed bundle unchanged. Each call still reloads rules/configs and evaluates the payload. The engine handles Claude file tools and Bash, Codex patch headers, and capy's three execution tools without executing submitted code. Every channel uses a stable project root for policy; the execution directory is separate.

scripts/generate-guard.sh projects the declaration into Claude's native secrets deny list, Codex's five unconditional native forbids, and the marked configuration tables. It copies the engine, launcher, wrapper, declaration and license byte-for-byte into kodex-guard/scripts/guard/. The release payload carries Claude's generated deny list in kk/baseline/claude/deny.json and the native Codex rules in kk/baseline/codex/kk.rules. make generate-guard regenerates these artifacts; structure checks and CI freshness checks reject drift. This generator is separate from Codex skill/agent generation.

The Claude plugin loads its own baseline, including on plugin-only installs. Codex receives the shared engine through the standalone guard plugin. The plugin anchors policy to the hook’s working directory, using the Git top level when available. Capy's own hooks retain their registration and routing responsibilities. Project .claude/kk-guard.json adds restrictions; user ~/.claude/kk-guard.json supplies scoped destructive/self-modification exceptions. Neither removes secrets. When installed, native Codex forbids take precedence over guard exceptions.

Legacy projects may still have both project hooks and plugin hooks. Wrapped Claude carries a native secrets deny list. The Codex guard checks registered shell, patch and capy calls, including file reads through the shell. See ADR 0012 for the decision and trade-offs, configuration for user controls, and testing for evidence limits.

docs.title: Plugin Graph Analysis (cmd/plugin-graph/)
docs.text:
A Go tool that builds a directed dependency graph of klaude-plugin/ and reports complexity metrics, impact analysis, and structural health. It gives maintainers and review skills a measured view of the skill web rather than a felt one.

It discovers six edge types across the plugin's link taxonomy: markdown links, symlinks, ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} template references, parameterized navigation paths (<name>/<phase>/<checklist> expanded over known sets), agent delegations (subagent_type table rows), and /kk: skill/command invocations. Edges use a dual-layer model — raw file endpoints drive broken-edge validation, while endpoints normalized to the owning artifact node drive metrics (fan-in/out, depth, transitive closure, coupling). Intra-artifact self-references are suppressed from the metric graph.

Subcommands: graph (emit the graph), metrics (complexity numbers), validate (broken-edge/orphan gate, exit 1 on findings). Output formats: text, json, dot, mermaid. Global --root selects the plugin directory; --ref <git-ref> analyzes a past commit via a throwaway git worktree. graph/metrics support targeted mode (positional args slice the graph to nodes reachable from a start set); validate rejects targets because its findings are whole-graph health signals.

Broken-edge detection exempts non-operative sources — links from evals/ fixtures (deliberately partial) and example-*.md templates — mirroring the orphan-detection evals/ exemption. Run via make plugin-graph (Go tests + validate against the real plugin); see Testing.

docs.title: Interactive field guide
docs.text:
Explore shows what the toolbox caught while building capy, a project built with it from start to finish. Each chapter tells one real catch: a short story, then a terminal pane with the /kk: command and the exact excerpt from capy's records, with the key phrase highlighted and every line number linked to the source on GitHub.

The page is an ordinary MkDocs page with the custom docs/overrides/explore.html template; there is no frontend build. All content is data in the front matter of docs/explore/index.md (explore.chapters and explore.closing), rendered server-side by the template, so the page is complete without JavaScript. Page-local explore.css lays out the copy column and the pane (stacked below 960px) in the site's Tokyo Night terminal style; explore.js only reveals each excerpt as its chapter reaches the middle of the viewport and keeps #<chapter-id> in the URL. prefers-reduced-motion turns the reveal off.

To edit or add a chapter, edit the front matter; the comment at its top lists the rules. Excerpts must be the record's exact text: mark cuts with …, the highlight with [[…]], and give the source line or range in at, which also builds the GitHub link. When a record describes a review but doesn't quote the command, set inferred: true; the pane says so. Run make docs-serve and open /explore/ to preview it.

The closing figures (capy's commits, ADRs and finished feature records) are counted at deploy time. The docs workflow makes a blob-less clone of capy and exports CAPY_STATS_REPO; the MkDocs hook scripts/mkdocs/capy_stats.py counts from it and writes the figures and the build date into the page. Without that variable, as in local builds, or when the clone or the counts fail, the page shows the snapshot figures and as-of date from the front matter, and CI reports the reason as a warning annotation rather than blocking the deploy. Figures refresh only when the docs deploy, and each released docs version keeps the figures it was built with; the as-of date says which. To try it locally, run CAPY_STATS_REPO=../capy/.git make docs-build.

docs.title: Installation Modes
docs.text:
Mode Installation and update owner Machine-managed install.sh bootstraps kk. kk upgrade selects one active release for the account and kk rollback restores a retained release. Plugin-only The vendor manages the Git-marketplace plugins and the user’s own vendor settings. Legacy template Until migration, the repository keeps its committed settings and sync infrastructure. Ordinary sync updates them. Only the explicit retirement step removes them.

A source checkout is also supported as input to ./install.sh --local . or kk upgrade --local .. It follows the same staging and activation path.

docs.title: Marketplace gotchas
docs.text:
Plugin source paths must use "./", not "." In marketplace.json, the source field for each plugin entry must use "./" (with trailing slash) for repo-root plugins, not bare ".". Claude Code's path resolver does not treat them equivalently — "." causes plugin install to fail with a misleading "source type not supported" error. Paths to subdirectories (e.g., "./klaude-plugin") already include the "./" prefix and are unaffected.

Stale marketplace cache after fixing. Claude Code caches cloned marketplace repos under ~/.claude/plugins/. After fixing marketplace.json and pushing, marketplace add or marketplace update may still use the stale cache. For a clean slate: remove the marketplace entry from ~/.claude/plugins/marketplaces/<name>/, delete any references in ~/.claude/plugins/known_marketplaces.json and ~/.claude/plugins/installed_plugins.json, then re-add with claude plugin marketplace add.

docs.title: Plugin Development
docs.text: The kk plugin lives at klaude-plugin/. This section covers the practical rules for authoring each component. For the full specification, see AGENTS.md.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text: Each skill is a directory under klaude-plugin/skills/<name>/ containing at minimum a SKILL.md entry point.

docs.title: SKILL.md structure
docs.text:
---
name: skill-name
description: |
  Trigger-first description. Front-load the key use case.
---

# Skill Title

## Conventions
## Workflow

docs.title: Naming rules
docs.text:
• Imperative verbs over noun phrases: /kk:design not /kk:analysis-process.
  • Family prefixes for grouped skills: /kk:review-code, /kk:review-design, /kk:review-spec.
  • Always use /kk: prefix when referencing skills: write /kk:review-code not review-code. The codex generation tool rewrites /kk: → $kk: for Codex output.

docs.title: Description budget
docs.text: Claude Code truncates skill descriptions at 1,536 characters per entry. OpenCode's limit is 1,024. Lead with trigger keywords — truncation happens at the tail. Detailed rules, cascades, and examples belong in the SKILL.md body, not the description.

docs.title: Workflow ordering (ADR 0004)
docs.text:
Every skill MUST fully load its instructions before taking any action on its subject matter. This is the single most critical rule for skill authoring.

  • "Instructions" = SKILL.md + referenced process files + shared protocols + resolved profile content.
  • "Action on subject matter" = reading diff content, editing code, engaging with idea prose, running tests, producing findings.
  • A narrow early scope is permitted (e.g., git diff --stat for filenames) to drive profile detection.
  • Content-level read instructions appear exactly once in the workflow, after instruction loading.

Every skill's Workflow section must carry a mandatory-order directive at the top naming this rule by intent. The failure mode: once an LLM has diff content loaded, it has enough to pattern-match findings without methodology, and its efficiency bias favors the shortcut. The methodology becomes ceremony the agent optimizes away.

docs.title: Shared Instructions
docs.text:
Instructions consumed by multiple skills live at klaude-plugin/skills/_shared/<name>.md. Each consuming skill gets a symlink:

# In the consuming skill directory:
ln -s ../_shared/<name>.md shared-<name>.md

Reference in skill prose as [shared-<name>.md](shared-<name>.md). The shared- prefix makes it obvious which files are shared vs. skill-specific. Only symlink into skills that actually reference the file.

Symlinks must stay inside the skills/ tree — cross-boundary symlinks break under some plugin installers (see ADR 0003).

docs.title: Plugin Content Is Self-Contained
docs.text: klaude-plugin/ ships standalone via the plugin marketplace — consumers get the plugin tree only, never this repo's docs/. Skill, agent, and profile prose must never reference toolbox-repo documents: no "(ADR NNNN)" citations, no links into this repo's docs/adr/ or docs/feat/wip|done/. For a consumer these are unresolvable at best; at worst they collide with the consumer repo's own ADR numbering and point to unrelated decisions. State each rule and its rationale in full in the plugin file itself; the back-reference lives on the repo side (the ADR cites the operative plugin files, not the other way around). Consumer-repo paths as behavioral targets (e.g. /kk:review-architecture accepting artifacts from the consumer's docs/adr/) are correct and expected.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Commands live under klaude-plugin/commands/<name>/. For skills with standard + isolated modes:

  • default.md — standard variant, invoked as /kk:<name>:default
  • isolated.md — isolated sub-agent variant, invoked as /kk:<name>:isolated

docs.title: Agents
docs.text:
Agent definitions live at klaude-plugin/agents/<name>.md with frontmatter specifying name, description, and tools (an allowlist of tools the agent can use):

---
name: code-reviewer
description: |
  Independent code reviewer with no authorship attachment.
tools:
  - Read
  - Grep
  - Glob
  - mcp__capy__capy_search
---

Agent names describe the role (code-reviewer, design-reviewer), not the skill that invokes them. Don't rename agent files when renaming skills.

Agents inherit the instruction-before-action rule — they must read provided checklists before analyzing subject matter, regardless of payload delivery order from the spawning skill.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text:
Hook definitions in klaude-plugin/hooks/hooks.json:

{
  "hooks": {
    "SessionStart": [{
      "hooks": [{
        "type": "command",
        "command": "bash \"${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}\"/scripts/set-plugin-root.sh \"${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}\""
      }]
    }, {
      "matcher": "startup|resume|clear|compact",
      "hooks": [{
        "type": "command",
        "command": "bash \"${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}\"/scripts/session-instructions.sh"
      }]
    }],
    "PreToolUse": [{
      "matcher": "Bash|Read|Edit|Write|NotebookEdit|Grep|Glob|mcp__.+__capy_(execute|execute_file|batch_execute)",
      "hooks": [{
        "type": "command",
        "command": "\"${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}\"/scripts/guard/guard.sh",
        "timeout": 15,
        "onFailure": "block"
      }]
    }]
  }
}

The root export writes TOOLBOX_PLUGIN_ROOT to CLAUDE_ENV_FILE. A machine-managed hook takes the physical root of its own release. A Git-marketplace hook uses cpr.py to find the project’s installed version and falls back to the root supplied by Claude.

The instruction hook reads the Markdown shipped beside it. Edit those files in klaude-plugin/instructions/ and the statusline scripts in klaude-plugin/statusline/. Both ship in the Claude plugin.

Permission guard contract: Read the complete hook payload from stdin (tool_name, tool_input, cwd and optional permission_mode). scripts/guard/guard.sh buffers the bytes once and invokes guard.py under isolated Python. Ordinary allow is silent with exit 0; config warnings may emit only systemMessage. Deny emits hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision: "deny", its reason on stdout and stderr, and exit 2. Missing interpreters, crashes and invalid engine output must deny. Claude's onFailure: "block" handles hook launch failures and timeouts; it requires Claude Code 2.1.295+. See the configuration guide for runtime requirements and supported channels.

The declaration and engine in klaude-plugin/scripts/guard/ are canonical. Run make generate-guard to refresh the two Codex runtime copies, their licenses, both rules projections, Claude’s deny list and the marked documentation tables. make check-guard checks freshness in a clean checkout.

To develop this repository with an agent, the user adds a physical checkout path (or a parent covering worktrees) to ~/.claude/kk-guard.json:

{"version":1,"projects":{"/absolute/path/to/agentstakk":{"disable_selfmod":true}}}

Merge that entry into existing user configuration. This permits settings and guard-file edits without disabling secrets checks. The project file can only tighten policy; committing disable_selfmod there does not authorize edits. Without the user exception, even adding a permission allow entry to settings is blocked. Destructive operations remain governed by their separate category settings and Codex native rules.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
Profiles at klaude-plugin/profiles/<name>/ provide domain-specific content to every workflow phase. See the Profile Conventions section of AGENTS.md for the full specification.

Required files:

  • DETECTION.md — three mandatory section headings: ## Path signals, ## Filename signals, ## Content signals. All three must be present even if the body is empty. Optional: ## Design signals for pre-code detection.
  • overview.md — human-readable summary and dependency-lookup targets.

Phase subdirectories: review-code/, design/, implement/, test/, document/, review-spec/. Not every profile populates every phase. Each populated phase must have an index.md with always-load and conditional entries. Conditional entries need explicit Load if: clauses naming concrete diff properties — two agents evaluating the same diff must reach the same conclusion.

Bidirectional index invariant (enforced by test/test-plugin-structure.sh):

  • Forward: every markdown link in index.md resolves to a file on disk.
  • Reverse: every .md in the phase directory (except index.md) is referenced by the index.

An unreferenced .md inside a phase subdirectory is always a bug. Authoring notes belong in overview.md at the profile root, not inside phase subdirectories.

Adding a new profile checklist:

  1. Create the profile directory by copying an existing one as a template.
  2. Write DETECTION.md and overview.md.
  3. Populate the phase subdirectories the profile needs (each with index.md).
  4. Append the profile name to EXPECTED_PROFILES in test/test-plugin-structure.sh.
  5. Append the profile name to the Known Profiles list in klaude-plugin/skills/_shared/profile-detection.md.
  6. Run bash test/test-plugin-structure.sh and confirm green.

docs.title: Evaluations
docs.text:
Skills with non-trivial decision logic should ship evaluation scenarios under klaude-plugin/skills/<skill>/evals/. One directory per eval:

evals/<eval-name>/
  eval.json        # scenario definition
  test-files/      # real filesystem fixtures

eval.json schema:

{
  "id": 1,
  "name": "eval-name-kebab-case",
  "description": "What this eval tests.",
  "skills": ["skill-name"],
  "prompt": "The user prompt that triggers the skill.",
  "trap": "The failure hypothesis — what a model is likely to get wrong.",
  "files": ["test-files/foo.yaml"],
  "assertions": [
    { "id": "1.1", "text": "Specific, gradable behavior." }
  ]
}

Use real filesystem fixtures in test-files/, not inline JSON strings. Include at least one regression eval proving the skill does NOT activate when it shouldn't.

docs.title: ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} — Substitution Rules
docs.text:
The harness provides ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} resolving to the installed plugin's root. Understanding its substitution boundary is critical (ADR 0003):

Substituted at plugin-load time (safe to use freely):

  • SKILL.md files
  • agents/*.md files
  • hooks/*.json command strings
  • MCP config files

NOT substituted by the Read tool (the literal token reaches the agent):

  • Everything in skills/_shared/
  • Everything in profiles/
  • Any file an agent reads at runtime

For runtime-read files, prefer explicit content (e.g., hard-coded profile name lists) over the token. If the file must describe a plugin-root path, instruct the agent to construct it using the resolved prefix it already knows from SKILL.md.

TOOLBOX_PLUGIN_ROOT — runtime alternative. The SessionStart hook exports this env var into every Bash call. Unlike ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} (which is only substituted at plugin-load time), ${TOOLBOX_PLUGIN_ROOT} is available in the shell environment throughout the session. Use it in Bash commands when you need the plugin root at runtime — e.g., ls ${TOOLBOX_PLUGIN_ROOT}/profiles/.

Other rules:

  • Brace form required: ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} works, bare $CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT does NOT get substituted.
  • Glob won't work against these paths — it's cwd-scoped and returns 0 matches for outside-cwd absolute paths. Use Read with the resolved path instead.
  • To reference the variable name literally in prose, use bare $CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT or ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}.

docs.title: Capy Knowledge Protocol
docs.text:
Skills that interact with capy MCP tools use kk: namespaced source labels:

Label Contents kk:arch-decisions Architecture decisions, design rationale kk:review-findings Code review patterns, recurring issues kk:lang-idioms Language best practices from external sources kk:project-conventions Discovered project patterns kk:test-patterns Testing approaches, edge cases kk:debug-context Root causes, tricky bugs

Only index non-obvious learnings not derivable from reading the code or git history. Empty results are normal for new projects — proceed with standard guidelines.

docs.title: Common Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Workflow ordering is the #1 failure mode. If the agent sees subject matter before methodology, it shortcuts the methodology. Structure every workflow so instructions load first. See ADR 0004.

  2. Forgetting make generate-kodex. After editing anything in klaude-plugin/, the Codex variant drifts. CI checks this with make generate-kodex && git diff --exit-code kodex-plugin/ kk/baseline/codex/agents/.

  3. Orphan files in profile phase directories. Every .md file (except index.md) must be referenced by the phase's index.md. The bidirectional invariant test catches this.

  4. Symlinks outside skills/. Per-skill symlinks must point within the skills/ tree (../_shared/<name>.md). Cross-boundary symlinks break under some installers. Profile content uses ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} references instead.

  5. Skill description truncation. Descriptions are truncated from the tail. If your trigger keywords are at the end, the skill won't be matched. Lead with the use case.

  6. Stale Known Profiles list. When adding a profile, you must update both EXPECTED_PROFILES in the test file and the Known Profiles list in klaude-plugin/skills/_shared/profile-detection.md. The list is the runtime enumeration — consumers iterate it rather than walking the filesystem.

  7. Renaming skills. Update EXPECTED_SKILLS / EXPECTED_COMMANDS in tests. Don't rename agent files. Don't touch docs/feat/done/ (frozen history). Watch for substring collisions in sed operations.

  8. Vague Load if: clauses. Conditional entries in profile index.md must name concrete diff properties (field values, filenames, directory names) — not vague category labels. Two agents evaluating the same diff must reach the same conclusion.

docs.title: Running Tests
docs.text:
Run all test suites:

Use the project tools on your normal PATH. The structure checks need Python 3.11+ (tomllib) or the documented tomli fallback; the released-client handoff needs Mike Farah's yq as well as jq. When selecting another Python installation, prepend its directory instead of replacing PATH and hiding existing tools.

for test in test/test-*.sh; do $test; done

Run a single suite:

./test/test-plugin-structure.sh

docs.title: Test Suites
docs.text: Suite What it covers test-plugin-structure.sh Plugin/marketplace manifests, skills, commands, hooks, profiles, cross-references, kodex-plugin generated output validation test-codex-structure.sh Codex marketplace, project config and hooks, release agent TOMLs and native rules test-template-sync.sh Compatibility notice and handoff from the released RC4 client in local and staged CI modes test-semver-compare.sh Semver comparison logic used by release workflows test-cpr.sh Claude Plugin Root resolver — exact/fuzzy matching, project-path resolution cascade (project → user → last-installed), install-path validation, env var precedence, error handling test-guard.sh Python engine tests: glob/path semantics, shell parsing, configuration layers, patches, capy inputs and corpus replay test-hooks.sh Full guard wrapper transport, plugin-only protection, fail-closed cases, capy-wrapper degradation, Read/Bash p95 latency test-generate-guard.sh Generated settings/rules/docs, output stability, per-rule examples and invalid-marker rejection test-codex-hooks.sh Bash/patch/MCP adapter delegation, failure denial, workspace selection and per-event Capy handoff test-review-eval-staging.sh Fresh before/after/history and legacy fixture staging, path safety and evaluator-material exclusion test-review-instructions.sh Instruction-packet source completeness, routing inputs and path boundaries; does not establish actor compliance test-functional-review-tools.sh Extracted bundle/capture/receipt/grading utilities and archive inventory; runs from a temporary copy without historical evidence, using Python 3.11+

docs.title: Machine delivery tests
docs.text:
Run bash test/test-kk.sh for installer, launchers, lifecycle, guard trust, update notices and migration orchestration. It uses temporary homes and vendor fixtures. Run bash test/test-template-sync.sh for the legacy handoff to the compatibility notice. Fetch v0.26.0-rc.4 for the released-client cases. The full sync and removal suites remain in that tag. The machine-delivery.yml CI job also runs the guard and Codex adapter suites on Python 3.8 and the current Python.

For installation evidence, kk status --live starts fresh vendor sessions and expects the installed guard’s own denial of a public canary. Open-session behavior needs a session spanning the relevant transition. The tagged pilot also verifies that an ordinary sync still leaves the legacy guard in place before migration. The release workflows run the machine delivery and generated-guard checks before publication.

After documentation changes run make docs-build with the packages in requirements.txt available. This regenerates the embedded graph and runs strict MkDocs validation. Machine delivery decision

docs.title: Test Infrastructure
docs.text:
Tests use shared utilities from test/helpers.sh:

  • log_section, log_test — structured output
  • assert_equals, assert_contains, assert_file_exists — assertion helpers
  • log_pass, log_fail, log_skip — result reporting
  • print_summary — final pass/fail count

Test fixtures live in test/fixtures/. The retained functional-review utilities own small synthetic fixtures within their tests. Set FUNCTIONAL_REVIEW_PYTHON to an explicit Python 3.11+ interpreter when the default python3 is older. Codex hook cases derive from toolbox-only-hooks.json, so the legacy case stays independent of Capy registrations in the developer's live .codex/hooks.json.

docs.title: Writing Tests
docs.text:
Follow proportionate verification when choosing coverage and acceptance criteria; ADR 0010 records the rationale. Deterministic tests protect software contracts. Agent evaluations measure semantic outcomes with variability and evidence limits; each assertion is not automatically a release gate. Keep required repository checks, and expand verification only for a concrete risk or unresolved decision.

  • Add tests to the appropriate existing suite when possible
  • New suites follow the same pattern: source helpers.sh, use log_section/log_test/assert_*, end with print_summary
  • Structure tests check file existence and content invariants, not runtime behavior
  • The bidirectional index invariant (every link in index.md resolves, every .md in a phase dir is referenced) is enforced in test-plugin-structure.sh — adding profile content automatically gets tested

docs.title: Go Tests
docs.text:
The Go tools under cmd/ ship unit and integration tests:

go test ./cmd/generate-kodex/...   # Codex generation tool
go test ./cmd/plugin-graph/...     # plugin dependency-graph analyzer

cmd/generate-kodex tests also run as part of make generate-kodex.

cmd/plugin-graph tests run via make plugin-graph, which additionally runs go run ./cmd/plugin-graph --root klaude-plugin/ validate against the real plugin — a structural-health gate that exits non-zero on broken markdown/template links or orphaned content. It complements test-plugin-structure.sh's bidirectional index invariant: the structure test enforces profile index.md completeness, while plugin-graph validate catches broken links and orphans across the whole plugin. See Architecture › Plugin Graph Analysis.

docs.title: Validation Before Release
docs.text:
• Every test/test-*.sh suite must pass
  • make generate-kodex must leave kodex-plugin/ and kk/baseline/codex/agents/ clean (git diff --exit-code)
  • make generate-guard must leave the release deny list and native rules, kodex-guard/scripts/guard/, and docs/user-guide/configuration.md clean (git diff --exit-code)
  • make plugin-graph must pass (Go tests + validate exits 0 against klaude-plugin/)
  • Go tests must pass (go test ./...)

docs.title: Permission Guard Verification
docs.text:
Run the engine and wrapper separately when diagnosing a failure:

bash test/test-guard.sh
bash test/test-hooks.sh
bash test/test-codex-hooks.sh
bash test/test-generate-guard.sh

test/guard/test_guard.py imports the engine and replays test/fixtures/guard/corpus.jsonl. Rows carry expected decisions/categories, optional cwd/project roots and per-row configuration fixtures. They use a synthetic home and project; submitted commands are never executed. KK_GUARD_TEST_PYTHON selects the engine test interpreter. The Python floor is 3.8, with actual local runs on 3.9.6/macOS and 3.10.12/Linux; the 3.8 syntax check does not replace a 3.8 runtime run.

The wrapper suite times 100 Read calls and every active Bash corpus row, including process startup, validation and cleanup. It always reports both p95 values when the timing probes run. Targets are 30 ms for file tools and 50 ms for Bash; local gates fail at 60/100 ms respectively when CI is unset. With CI present, timing is reported without enforcement. A CI-mode pass is not evidence that a local latency target passed.

The 2026-10-26 macOS arm64 run with the default Apple Python 3.9.6 measured 76.62 ms Read / 76.00 ms Bash outside the agent sandbox: the Read gate failed and both targets were missed. The performance requirement remains open before feature completion; limits were not relaxed. See the permission-guard evidence for all attempts and prerequisites.

A later wrapper optimization on the same host prefers an existing Homebrew Python, skips unused site startup and avoids subprocesses for empty output. That run measured 40.92 ms Read / 42.13 ms Bash, passing both unchanged local gates and the Bash target. A second pass imports the engine through a small launcher so Python can reuse compiled bytecode: the unchanged benchmark measured 37.27 → 31.10 ms Read / 42.50 → 34.75 ms Bash against its immediate predecessor. The 30 ms Read target remains open. Earlier measurements remain historical evidence.

Launcher tests cover policy reloads between calls, unavailable caches, import isolation, source updates and loader failures. Cold starts and unwritable cache directories compile source. Apple Python 3.9.6 disables cache writes by default; its functional tests pass, with the corrupt-cache test explicitly skipped. The speedup was measured with Homebrew Python 3.15.1 and does not establish timing on other runtimes or hosts.

Final verification on Linux after the shell-path and escaped-literal corrections passed 96 engine tests on Python 3.10 and 3.12, the complete wrapper suite (51 cases / 248 assertions), and Codex adapter checks. Read/Bash p95 measured 23.66/41.59 ms with the unchanged local gates. The new regressions fail against the preceding engine and cover relative directory changes, wildcard matches and escaped interpreter paths, alongside benign and quoted/raw-literal controls. The current corrected engine still needs macOS timing; the user explicitly retained the 30 ms requirement.

Payload tests establish adapter contracts, not installed hook activation. Live probes must record versions, actual hook inputs/results and benign controls. The Claude bypass probe uses a disposable project outside temporary roots so rm -rf ./scratch is not intentionally exempt. Use synthetic files and an absent .env, never real credentials. The recorded Claude 2.1.296 probe denied both destructive and secrets access under bypass mode.

Codex 0.164.0 on macOS verified relative patch paths against cwd, first with inline hooks and then with project-file registration under normal config loading. The latter probe recorded one startup and two patch-hook invocations: the benign patch succeeded and the synthetic .env patch was denied. It used explicit project trust and a one-invocation hook-trust bypass for inspected definitions; persisted trust, interactive hook approval, restarts and other versions or hosts were not exercised. Two fresh --ignore-user-config probes recorded no hooks, including one with hooks explicitly enabled, so use normal config loading for this check. The isolated-mode cause remains tracked in #179 and the interactive trust lifecycle in #182; the full evidence and historical failed attempts remain in the feature's design §16.

docs.title: Agent evaluation
docs.text:
Skill evals live under each canonical klaude-plugin/skills/<skill>/evals/ directory. A scenario contains eval.json, subject files under test-files/ and optional grader-only expected results under oracle/. Regenerate the Codex copies with make generate-kodex.

The review harness describes component grading and full-workflow capture. Its setup.sh stages flat fixtures, complete before/ and after/ snapshots, and optional local Git history into fresh destinations. Use a workspace outside any SKILL.md ancestor so the host skill does not activate a profile on unrelated fixtures. Stage only subject files; keep assertions, oracles, grading controls and results outside actor inputs and filtered plugin bundles. Deliberately broken eval/template links must remain.

Run ordinary skill prompts against declared immutable instructions and fresh fixture/knowledge state. For targeted changes, compare with the immediate predecessor under matching conditions. Capture observable tool results, reviewer handoffs, initial/final files and final reports; do not substitute private reasoning or final self-attestation for execution. Never include credentials. Workflow grading uses sealed evidence; component grading uses the supplied output text. Calibrate the chosen grader against meaningful positive, negative and missing-evidence examples before making comparative claims.

Keep PASS/FAIL/PARTIAL observations separate from adoption. A material wrong verdict matters differently from optional advice, a missing endpoint name or an unavailable external reviewer. Retain all attempts and disclose sample size, runtime/configuration differences and missing coverage. Synthetic external-review replays test reporting, not live integration. Expand measurement only for a concrete uncertainty that could change the decision; structural tests do not establish model reliability.

The functional-review summary records the retained comparisons, current acceptance and known limits. Detailed captures remain in the feature's evidence tree until the human-owned release archive is verified.

docs.text: What Agentstakk caught while we were building capy, a Go MCP server built from start to finish with it: an agent that skipped its own review method, a design shaped by a recurring bug in capy's knowledge base, an upgrade that would have locked every existing vault, a deny-list bypass through a symlinked folder, tests that could chmod a developer's real key file, and live tests that never exercised the default wait. docs.text:
Install kk on your machine to use the workflow skills, guards and launcher settings across repositories. From a toolbox checkout, run ./install.sh --local ., put ~/.local/bin on your PATH, then run kk status. Start a session in your project with kk claude or kk codex.

If you already have… Next step An ordinary repository Start the launcher in its working tree. Using an existing project A repository with .github/template-state.json Verify the machine guards and preview what your team would lose or keep. Migrate the template Your own CLI configuration and a preference for vendor-managed plugins Install the workflow plugin directly from the Git marketplace. Plugin-only setup A working installation Run your first design and review. Try it

docs.title: Use kk in an existing repository
docs.text: Install kk once. In your project, run kk claude or kk codex. Keep versioned team instructions in CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md, project restrictions in .claude/kk-guard.json, and your personal launcher preferences in the machine override file.

docs.title: Repositories created from the toolbox template
docs.text:
Look for .github/template-state.json. Its presence identifies a repository managed by template sync. Installing kk leaves the repository files in place. Team members can install and verify kk before anyone commits changes.

When the team is ready, follow the migration guide. kk migrate verifies the guard for each tool the repository uses, previews an ordinary sync to the retirement release, then previews removal. You decide separately whether to apply each step. Review the uncommitted diff with collaborators, particularly if CI or cloud sessions depend on the committed plugin settings.

docs.title: Repositories using plugins directly
docs.text: The plugin-only setup remains available. When moving to the managed installation, kk status reports Git-marketplace copies. Check the scope before removing one. A project-scoped registration may also serve other developers or CI.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Agentstakk is a collection of "tools" for all your agentic workflows (currently supports claude-code and codex!) — pre-configured MCP servers, skills, sub-agents, commands, hooks, statuslines with themes, and more — everything you need for AI-powered development workflows, used and battle-tested daily on many of my own projects.

Important

This project was created with the help of Claude-Code. It is, however, always reviewed, tested, and reworked with a human-in-the-loop.

No AI slop here. Purely AI-made skills are hot garbage, and that's putting it mildly.

That said, if you have any problems with code that is written by AI — you've been warned. But, then again, why would you be interested in AI-related configs and skills in the first place... ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

docs.title: Why Agentstakk?
docs.text:
Tools like Claude Code and Codex are powerful on their own, but LLMs don't know your development workflow. This project started as a way to streamline configurations across projects without copy-paste. Over time, recurring patterns evolved into skills and agents.

A minimal, opinionated configuration — sensible permission baselines, a rich statusline, MCP server wiring, and a launcher that selects the same release across your projects. Think of it as a dotfiles repo for Claude Code and Codex.

A structured development pipeline — 16 workflow and utility skills with explicit multi-language support that take you from idea through design, implementation, code review, testing, to documentation, with persistent knowledge that carries across sessions.

/kk:design → /kk:review-design → /kk:implement → /kk:review-code → /kk:test → /kk:document

docs.title: Features at a Glance
docs.text:
• 16 workflow and utility skills — a complete development pipeline invoked as /kk:<skill-name>, plus utilities such as /kk:clarify-docs for existing documentation, PR drafts and issue descriptions
  • Multi-language support — precise and distinct instructions from design, to implementation, to testing, to review for: Go, Java, JS/TS, Kotlin, Kubernetes, and Python
  • Multi-model code review — independent reviewers using sub-agents and external models (Gemini, etc.)
  • Persistent knowledge base — findings, decisions, and conventions that survive across sessions via Capy
  • Up-to-date library docs — always-current documentation lookup via Context7
  • Battle-tested configuration — permissions, statusline themes, hooks, sensible defaults

docs.title: kk Plugin
docs.text:
The kk plugin contains all development workflow functionality — 16 skills, 5 commands, and hooks — distributed via the Claude Code plugin system (see kodex-plugin for the Codex variant). Skills are invoked as /kk:skill-name, commands as /kk:dir:command.

Alongside skills/, commands/, agents/, and hooks/, the plugin ships a top-level profiles/ directory. Each profile (e.g., go, python, k8s) bundles per-domain content — detection rules, review checklists, design prompts, test validators, doc rubrics — that the workflow skills consult when the code under work matches the profile. Profiles are the extension point for new languages and IaC DSLs.

For an existing bug report or feature request, optionally use /kk:clarify-docs with a local draft, pasted description or issue URL. It saves local edits, preserves uncertainty and respects the readers' access to supporting evidence. Implementing an issue uses /kk:implement. See issue-description examples for destinations, missing context and sharing boundaries.

docs.title: Machine configuration
docs.text: kk claude composes Claude preferences, native secret denies and a themed statusline for the session. kk codex selects the managed profile, and Codex loads the separately reviewed guard plugin. Your repositories keep their own instructions and settings. See Configuration.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: The installation guide lists the required tools. MCP integrations are optional. Configure them when you need library documentation, external reviews or persistent project memory. MCP servers

docs.text:
• Context7 API key — for library documentation lookups
  • Gemini API key for Pal (or any other provider) — for multi-model code review through API models. Optional: without one, isolated reviews use your installed CLIs (Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity) through Pal's clink; see MCP Servers → Pal

docs.text: Examples of actual Claude Code workflows executed using this template's configs, skills, and tools: examples/

docs.title: Plugin-Only Setup
docs.text: Install just the plugin to get all 16 workflow and utility skills. The commands below apply once the renamed public marketplace is published. Until then, use serpro69/claude-toolbox as the repository and claude-toolbox as the marketplace ID.

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
claude plugin marketplace add serpro69/agentstakk
claude plugin install kk@agentstakk

Skills are available as /kk:(skill-name) (annotated with (kk) in the slash command menu). The Claude plugin also includes commands, sub-agents and the permission guard. The guard protects secrets, destructive operations and configuration on Bash, file tools and capy execution tools without needing template settings or configuration files.

Use Claude Code 2.1.295+, Bash, jq and Python 3.8+. Guard failures block matched calls, including reads; repair a missing interpreter rather than expecting the hook to skip it. See Guard Configuration for project additions and user exceptions. Disabling hooks removes plugin-only protection because this installation mode has no native settings baseline.

For launchers, native permission settings and machine-wide updates, use Install kk. Configure MCP servers separately.

docs.title: Codex
docs.text:
codex plugin marketplace add serpro69/agentstakk
codex plugin add kk@agentstakk

The Codex plugin includes skills and language-specific profile content (review checklists, implementation gotchas, etc.). See kodex-plugin for details.

To install the separate permission guard from a marketplace revision that includes it, run codex plugin add kk-guard@agentstakk. Review its three PreToolUse handlers in /hooks. The guard reads project policy from the session workspace.

Machine installation also supplies the named Codex profile, owned sub-agent files and optional account-wide rules.

For MCP servers (Context7, Pal), see Codex MCP Setup.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text: Use the vendor’s marketplace update commands for the Git installation. In Claude Code, refresh the marketplace with claude plugin marketplace update agentstakk, update kk@agentstakk with claude plugin update kk@agentstakk, and start a fresh session. In Codex, review changed guard handlers in /hooks before using a new session. Managed installations use kk upgrade.

docs.title: Switch an existing Git-marketplace installation
docs.text:
Use these steps after the public marketplace identifies itself as agentstakk. The old registration is named claude-toolbox. The repository address and marketplace ID are separate vendor settings.

  1. List the installed plugins and their scopes. Add the new Git marketplace with claude plugin marketplace add serpro69/agentstakk or codex plugin marketplace add serpro69/agentstakk.
  2. Install the replacement with claude plugin install kk@agentstakk or codex plugin add kk@agentstakk. If you use the public Codex guard, also run codex plugin add kk-guard@agentstakk and review its handlers in plain Codex.
  3. Remove the old copies you own. For a Claude user install, run claude plugin uninstall --scope user --keep-data kk@claude-toolbox. For Codex, run codex plugin remove kk@claude-toolbox and, if installed, codex plugin remove kk-guard@claude-toolbox. Once nothing else uses that registration, run claude plugin marketplace remove --scope user claude-toolbox or codex plugin marketplace remove claude-toolbox. Update any project-owned enablement in its original scope.
  4. Start a fresh session and check that only the intended guard is enabled.

docs.title: What's Included
docs.text:
The plugin gives you:

  • 16 workflow and utility skills — /kk:design, /kk:implement, /kk:review-code, /kk:clarify-docs, etc.
  • Language profiles — Go, Java, JS/TS, Kotlin, Kubernetes, Python
  • Commands — isolated variants for code review, CoVe and spec review
  • Hooks — permission checks for Claude Code and, with the separate guard plugin, for Codex
  • Sub-agents — independent reviewers (Claude Code only)

docs.title: What's Not Included
docs.text:

  • Native permission-settings baseline and statusline (the Claude guard's runtime baseline is included)
  • The kk launchers, offline rollback and owned Codex agent files

For the full setup, install kk on your machine.

docs.title: Try It
docs.text:
After installation, open a terminal in your project and run kk claude. In Codex, use kk codex and invoke the same skills as $kk:design, $kk:implement and so on. The examples below use Claude Code.

For an optional conversation first, use /kk:brainstorm to explore a technical idea or decision. The interview adapts to what you need to decide and ends with a chat-only recap of decisions, rationale, and open assumptions. It creates no files and does not start another workflow automatically. Request /kk:design when you want written planning.

  1. Write a plan. Type /kk:design and describe a feature you want to build. Claude will ask refinement questions and confirm decisions, then produce design docs, an implementation plan, and a task list in docs/feat/wip/.

  2. Review the design. Run /kk:review-design your-feature to catch gaps before writing code.

  3. Build it. Type /kk:implement — Claude executes the task list with code review checkpoints between batches.

  4. Review the code. /kk:review-code checks for SOLID violations, security risks, and quality issues. Use /kk:review-code:isolated for independent sub-agent reviewers with zero authorship bias.

This is the core loop. See the kk plugin README for all available skills and the full workflow pipeline.

docs.title: What Just Happened?
docs.text:
The planning and implementation loop passes artifacts between skills. Optional brainstorming supplies conversation context:

Skill Input Output /kk:brainstorm (optional) A technical idea or decision Chat recap; no files /kk:design Your idea, optionally with a brainstorm recap design.md, implementation.md, tasks.md /kk:review-design Design docs Review findings, gap analysis /kk:implement Task list Code changes, review checkpoints /kk:review-code Git diff Findings, fix suggestions /kk:test Code changes Test files, coverage report /kk:document All of the above Updated architecture.md, ADRs

docs.title: Install kk on your machine
docs.text: Install once per user account. You can then start Claude Code or Codex in any repository with the same toolbox release. New projects need no toolbox files.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
On macOS or Linux, use Bash, Git, jq, Python 3.8 or later, and a signed-in Claude Code CLI with plugin support (2.1.295 or later). Install Codex first if you also want its managed profile and plugins. The installer validates the release and registers its local marketplace with each supported CLI it finds. Claude Code is required for this installer.

From a toolbox checkout that contains install.sh, run the following from its root. This works before the first machine release is published.

./install.sh --local .

Once the first stable machine release (v0.26.0) is published, you can install the latest stable version without a checkout:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/serpro69/agentstakk/master/install.sh | bash

For a reproducible install, fetch install.sh from the chosen tag and pass --version TAG to it. For a pre-release, name the full candidate tag rather than selecting the latest stable release.

Put ~/.local/bin on your shell’s PATH. For example, run export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" and add that line to your shell profile for future terminals. The installer creates the kk entry point there. By default releases live in ${XDG_DATA_HOME:-$HOME/.local/share}/kk. Set KK_HOME before installation to choose another directory. If the first install is interrupted, rerun the installer to resume.

docs.title: Move an existing installation to Agentstakk
docs.text:
After the hosted rename, update the Git remote of a clone that tracks the upstream repository. Keep a fork’s origin pointing to the fork. If the canonical remote is named upstream, use that name instead of origin.

git remote set-url origin https://github.com/serpro69/agentstakk.git

docs.title: RC4 marketplace switch
docs.text:
RC4 registered the directory KK_HOME as toolbox in both vendors. The renamed release registers that same directory as agentstakk-local. Keep your existing KK_HOME, Codex home, overrides and profile. Close old sessions and finish batches before removing their registrations. Start new sessions after checking the replacement.

  1. Stage the published release with KK_REPOSITORY=serpro69/agentstakk kk upgrade --version TAG. Use the exact candidate or stable tag in a terminal. Confirm the guard identity change while the RC4 registrations are still installed. Declining leaves them active. While the pilot catalogs are registered, the new installer leaves the candidate staged and identifies the vendor to switch.

  2. Inspect claude plugin list --json, claude plugin marketplace list --json, codex plugin list --json and codex plugin marketplace list --json. The pilot's local marketplace root should be your KK_HOME. The following commands apply to its user-scope plugins. Skip entries the vendor inventory shows as absent. Remove a marketplace only after checking that no other plugin or scope uses its registration. Leave project-owned enablement in its original scope. Skip the Codex commands on a Claude-only install. Run the Codex commands with the same CODEX_HOME used for installation. If kk identifies another recorded Codex home, inspect it separately.

    claude plugin uninstall --scope user --keep-data kk@toolbox
claude plugin marketplace remove --scope user toolbox
codex plugin remove kk@toolbox
codex plugin remove kk-guard@toolbox
codex plugin marketplace remove toolbox

  3. Run kk upgrade to resume the same staged and confirmed release. In plain Codex, review the three kk-guard@agentstakk-local handlers in /hooks. Then run kk apply and kk status --live. The launcher reports pending review until Codex trusts the new identity. An old public plugin still enabled by a project will appear in status. Update that setting in its original scope.

If you stop after removing the pilot registrations while the new release is still staged, the RC4 catalogs still exist under KK_HOME. To stay on RC4, add that directory back with each vendor’s plugin marketplace add command and reinstall the user-scope kk@toolbox plugins and Codex’s kk-guard@toolbox. Check kk status and review any hooks the vendor requests. Once activation has started, use kk upgrade to resume. If you choose recovery instead, follow the cross-name cleanup below before invoking the printed rollback command. During an interrupted activation that command restores the still-active release, which can differ from the usual rollback target.

Offline rollback across the rename. Check the rollback target in kk status. To restore RC4, close sessions and use the five commands above with agentstakk-local in place of toolbox to remove the departing registrations. Then run kk rollback. RC4 runs its own installer and restores @toolbox from its retained files. Check both vendor inventories and plain Codex’s hook status before resuming work. RC4 cannot diagnose newer duplicate registrations. To return to a retained renamed release, remove the RC4 registrations as above and run kk rollback again when the renamed release is the recorded target. Review any handlers the vendor marks untrusted or modified. A live check requires an available model transport.

Legacy repository migration still uses the full template at v0.26.0-rc.4.

For a Git-marketplace installation, follow the plugin-only switch.

docs.title: Verify and launch
docs.text:
kk status
kk claude

For Codex, start plain codex without --profile in your project. Review the folder’s trust prompt and the three managed kk-guard handlers in /hooks (@toolbox through RC4, @agentstakk-local in the renamed release). Exit Codex. These decisions are now in your account configuration. Use kk codex for daily sessions. When a new project needs a folder trust decision, make it in plain codex there first. If Codex reports that it cannot read hook trust, run kk apply interactively and acknowledge the review. That vendor state is recorded as unverified. Run kk status --live from your terminal. It starts short vendor sessions in scratch workspaces and checks for a denial from each managed guard. It needs working vendor authentication.

If you already installed plugins from the Git marketplace, kk status lists the copies and their scopes. kk status --remove-mixed offers to remove user-scope Git copies with a managed counterpart. Review project-owned registrations in their repository. Existing repositories

docs.title: Update and recover
docs.text:
kk upgrade                      # latest stable machine release
kk upgrade --check              # report availability without changing the installation
kk upgrade --version v0.26.0    # choose a published machine release
kk upgrade --local .            # use the current toolbox checkout
kk status
kk rollback                     # restore the recorded target offline

After an interrupted upgrade, kk status gives the resume or rollback command. Save the recovery command printed during an upgrade. It invokes the retained release’s own dispatcher, so it also works if the newly active command is damaged. Restart long-running sessions within 14 days after their release is superseded.

Managed Codex batch runs (kk codex exec and kk codex review) can run concurrently. Each holds its verified installation until the vendor process exits. If a batch is running, an upgrade can stage its release and asks you to retry activation afterward with kk upgrade. The same retry applies to kk apply and kk rollback. To cancel a supervised batch, use Ctrl-C in its terminal or send SIGTERM. Killing only the supervisor with SIGKILL can leave the vendor running. Interactive sessions continue to use the existing upgrade and hook-review behavior.

Transition from the pilot releases. Finish running batches before upgrading from or rolling back to v0.26.0-rc.1 through rc.3. Those releases predate batch coordination. Check the rollback target in kk status. If it is a Claude-only pilot release and the departing release added Codex, its recovery code can leave the departing Codex plugins installed. Full batch coordination and automatic removal of those plugins apply when both releases contain the correction.

Next, try the workflow, configure your launchers, or migrate a legacy repository.

docs.title: Claude Code authentication and terms

kk claude starts the Claude Code executable you installed and passes a local settings file with --settings. Claude Code loads the toolbox skills and hooks through its plugin system. Sign in through Claude Code using your own account or your organization's configured provider. The launcher leaves authentication and billing with that provider. Claude Code authentication · Claude Code plugins

Anthropic’s published guidance allows end users to sign in to the unmodified Claude Code binary with their own subscription. Agentstakk uses that flow for local subscription use. It supplies settings and plugins while Claude Code handles sign-in with the provider and usage is billed under the user’s or organization’s agreement. Anthropic lists consumer terms for individual plans and commercial terms for Team, Enterprise and API use. Products or hosted services that run Claude Code have additional requirements, including preserving its sign-in methods and direct billing to each end user. The user-scope plugin kk@agentstakk-local supplies guard hooks wherever Claude loads and enables it. It checks shell calls, Claude file tools and the supported capy execution tools. Use Claude Code 2.1.295+ with Bash, jq and Python 3.8+. Start a fresh session after an upgrade. Guard configuration

Wrapped sessions also receive the native secret deny list through kk claude, including when you supply your own --settings. They get the toolbox statusline in trusted interactive sessions with hooks enabled. Inspect the composed settings with kk claude --print-layer.

Unwrapped sessions such as bare claude, the IDE extension and the desktop app can load the plugin hooks. They do not receive the launcher’s native deny list or statusline. A user-level install on your machine does not reach cloud sessions or fresh CI runners. Provision the plugin on those hosts or retain the relevant committed enablement when migrating.

docs.title: Codex
docs.text: Install kk with Codex on your PATH, then start kk codex in your project. The managed marketplace provides two plugins. kk@agentstakk-local supplies workflow skills and profiles. kk-guard@agentstakk-local supplies the guard adapters and runtime, with its own version and trust history. For a Git-marketplace installation, use plugin-only setup.

docs.title: Permission guard
docs.text:
Start plain codex without --profile, open /hooks, and review the three managed PreToolUse handlers (Bash, Edit/Write and capy execution). Exit and start a fresh kk codex session. Run kk status --live for a scratch-session check. A skills-only upgrade reuses the installed guard when its content is unchanged.

Two open-session cases need attention. Close Codex sessions before confirming a guard-changing upgrade or rollback. An open session can lose protection across the change. Review the replacement hooks and start a fresh session before resuming work. Also close sessions opened in a legacy repository before kk was installed and reviewed: they depend on repository scripts that migration removes. Migrate a template repository

For exec and review, the launcher reads trust and enablement for the selected workspace. Missing, modified, disabled or untrusted handlers block a batch launch. Batch launches also require a verifiable local workspace and the managed profile. Use plain Codex for account-wide hook review. An interactive launch can also select another named profile. If the vendor lacks the trust-reading method, review the hooks and run kk apply interactively to acknowledge that review. The recorded state is unverified, and batch launches warn. kk migrate also requires an attributable live denial.

Run kk apply after edits.

Precedence is base user settings, selected profile, trusted project settings, then explicit CLI flags. Bare Codex uses its normal profile selection. The user-scope guard plugin can still run there once trusted. Toolbox checks for collisions before creating owned files.

Approval policy, approval reviewer and sandbox defaults are optional. The separate native-forbids opt-in affects every repository and bare session using this Codex home. Existing project sandbox and approval settings still win after migration. Override keys and effects

docs.title: Where Codex saves trust decisions
docs.text:
Codex 0.171.0 saves interactive hook and folder trust in the active configuration file. Plain codex saves those choices in $CODEX_HOME/config.toml; kk codex selects the generated $CODEX_HOME/kk.config.toml. Use plain Codex for machine guard review, including after a guard change, and for the first folder trust decision in each repository. Project restrictions still apply.

If you already made a decision in the wrapped session, exit it and open plain codex in the same directory. Confirm the folder and hook choices you actually intend at account scope. Then run kk apply to regenerate the owned profile and kk status --live to verify. Regeneration replaces profile-local edits. Toolbox never copies a trust decision into another scope. Codex also writes display counters for model tips when its TUI opens. The launcher accepts those counters while continuing to verify the generated settings before batch runs.

docs.title: Repository instructions
docs.text:
Codex loads the root AGENTS.md. For an extra file to reach a wrapped session, add a repository-relative path on its own line outside a code fence, for example:

@.claude/CLAUDE.team.md
@.capy/AGENTS.md

On an interactive launch, kk codex shows the eligible paths and sizes and asks once per repository and path list. A changed list requires a new decision. Approved imports are reread on launch and added to the toolbox’s developer instructions for that session, replacing any repository-level developer_instructions value. Without prior approval, non-interactive launches skip the imports. The wrapper expands one level of imports. Bare Codex does not expand these references. Missing, protected, oversized or outside-repository files are skipped with a diagnostic.

docs.title: Project instruction budget
docs.text: The managed profile sets project_doc_max_bytes = 65536 for native project instructions. Set a different budget in codex.settings and run kk apply. The launcher separately limits its serialized import argument to 120 KiB including toolbox text and escaping.

docs.title: Removed Auto-review settings
docs.text:
Current Codex versions warn that auto_review.experimental_policy_template and auto_review.extra_policy are ignored. The toolbox template no longer ships the [auto_review] block that supplied these settings for Codex 0.164.0. Check older template repositories for these obsolete entries. For an immediate manual fix, remove those two keys and their complete multiline values from .codex/config.toml; remove the table header too if it becomes empty.

The old block supplied a standing authorization for read-only external Claude reviews. Removing ignored settings clears the warning; it does not restore that authorization. Approval and sandbox defaults in the machine profile are separate opt-ins.

Codex's warning directs additional Guardian rules to the top-level guardian_extra_policy key in managed requirements.toml. On Linux and macOS, the system file is /etc/codex/requirements.toml; project-local and user-local requirements.toml files are not documented managed sources. See managed configuration. The machine installer leaves this system policy to administrators. Any migration must retain the intended review scope and existing managed requirements, then verify the effective policy in a fresh session.

auto_review.policy remains supported, but it replaces the entire policy. Putting only the old authorization paragraph there would discard the other policy rules. See Auto-review configuration.

If you use pal and rely on clink-based reviews, but they get blocked by the auto-review policy, the current recommended solution is to add the following to your /etc/codex/requirements.toml:

guardian_extra_policy="""
## Pre-authorized external code reviews

For work requested by the user in the current project, PAL clink calls using
cli_name="claude", role="default", and allow_edits=false are authorized for
independent code and technical-document review. Treat Anthropic through the
configured Claude CLI as an approved recipient for this purpose.

This standing authorization covers successive tasks, revised snapshots,
review-fix follow-ups, and the source, diffs, tests, documentation, review
criteria, provenance metadata, and relevant local dependency source needed
for the review. Temporary review bundles containing those materials are
included. Do not require separate disclosure approval for each snapshot.

The request must instruct the reviewer to inspect files without modifying
project files or running tests, builds, or submitted code. Read-only inspection
commands are permitted. This authorization excludes credentials, secret files,
production data, unrelated personal information, and unrelated repositories.
Other destinations, clients, purposes, and actions remain subject to the normal
approval policy. Preserve all other safety rules and managed restrictions.
"""

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: The machine installation supplies a Claude launch layer and a named Codex profile. Repositories can keep their own settings, instructions and project guard policy.

docs.title: How Configuration Works
docs.text:
Edit ${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-$HOME/.config}/kk/config.json for personal toolbox preferences. All keys are optional. Merge the keys you need into an existing file.

{
  "launchNotice": false,
  "claude": {
    "defaults": {"skills": false},
    "optIn": {"webSearch": true},
    "settings": {"effortLevel": "medium"}
  },
  "codex": {
    "settings": {"model_reasoning_effort": "high"}
  }
}

Claude. Each kk claude launch builds a settings layer. The default effort is high. Baseline preferences yield to explicit user, project and local values, including individual environment variables. The baseline leaves model selection to Claude or the adopter. You can supply claude.settings and a claude.settingsFile path (relative to the override file or absolute). The file takes precedence over claude.settings for scalar preferences. A caller’s own --settings is composed too. The launcher appends the generated native secret denies to the final layer. Inspect it with kk claude --print-layer.

Claude permission or preference Machine default Skill(kk:*) Standing authorization for model-initiated calls to every matching skill, including skills added by future releases. Set claude.defaults.skills to false to review skill use individually. Read access to the active release Lets skills and reviewers read their bundled criteria. Set claude.defaults.readRelease to false to opt out. PAL needs a separate grant for its temporary review files. Bash(mkdir:*) and WebSearch Opt in separately with claude.optIn.mkdir and claude.optIn.webSearch. The legacy grants for cat, grep, ls and sort are dropped. Statusline and instructions The launcher supplies the statusline in trusted interactive wrapped sessions with hooks enabled. Set claude.defaults.statusLine to false to opt out. The plugin supplies behavioral instructions at session start and supports claude.instructions.

Codex. kk codex selects the kk profile. It takes precedence over base user configuration and yields to trusted project configuration and explicit CLI flags. codex.settings can set profile values. Configure hook and plugin enablement in native Codex settings. After editing overrides, run kk apply to regenerate the active release’s owned files offline. kk status and kk codex report pending edits.

There are two independent opt-ins:

  1. Approval and sandbox defaults. Enable the values you want under codex.optIn: "approval_policy": true supplies on-request, "approvals_reviewer": true supplies user, and "sandbox_mode": true supplies read-only. Otherwise the machine owner’s native settings govern. Migrated repositories keep their existing three project values until someone removes them.
  2. Account-wide native forbids. Set "nativeForbids": true under codex.optIn and run kk apply to install $CODEX_HOME/rules/kk.rules. Those rules apply to bare Codex and unrelated repositories using that Codex home. Project settings and guard exceptions cannot loosen a native forbid. Switch it off and run kk apply to remove the toolbox-owned file.

Machine updates replace the previous per-repository sync PRs. Review the chosen release before upgrading. A local user install covers sessions that load its plugin. Hosts without it, including fresh CI runners and cloud sessions, need separate provisioning if migration removes committed plugin enablement. See the migration guide for team-wide effects.

docs.title: Permission Baselines
docs.text:
The permission guard separates secrets, destructive operations and changes to its own configuration. Its baseline allows ordinary logs, dependencies, build output and .env.example; projects can add their own restrictions. A settings allow entry cannot override a secrets deny.

The tables below are generated from klaude-plugin/scripts/guard/guard-rules.json with make generate-guard. The hook enforces the shared declaration. Wrapped Claude sessions also receive the native deny list. Project additions belong in .claude/kk-guard.json. Keep per-repository MCP tool permissions in .claude/settings.local.json.

Self-modification protection also blocks an agent from adding an allow entry to .claude/settings.json or .claude/settings.local.json. The disable_selfmod example below lets the user authorize those edits for a chosen project; it does not loosen secrets.
