The hook exempts literal rm targets strictly beneath its temporary roots: /tmp, /private/tmp, /var/folders, /private/var/folders, $TMPDIR. Secrets and protected configuration still apply. Codex native rules forbid rm even for temporary targets.

docs.title: Protected configuration
docs.text:
The guard blocks mutations of these paths, including moving their parent directories:

  • .claude/settings.json
  • .claude/settings.local.json
  • .claude/kk-guard.json
  • ~/.claude/settings.json
  • ~/.claude/settings.local.json
  • ~/.claude/kk-guard.json
  • .codex/hooks.json
  • .codex/rules/**
  • .codex/scripts/**
  • ~/.claude/plugins/**
  • $KK_HOME/**
  • $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/kk/config.json
  • Each path recorded in $KK_HOME/state.json under installed_paths, including the ~/.local/bin/kk launcher, the installed Codex profile, the opt-in rules file and toolbox sub-agents.
  • $CODEX_HOME/plugins/cache/**

The toolbox home defaults to ${XDG_DATA_HOME:-~/.local/share}/kk. The configuration and Codex homes default to ~/.config and ~/.codex. A file in a shared directory becomes protected when the installer records its exact path. Reads still follow the secrets policy.

When copying an unrelated executable into ~/.local/bin/, name its destination file explicitly. A directory-only destination is checked as a parent of the protected kk launcher.

Project config may add paths under selfmod. To let an agent edit settings or guard files for one checkout, the user can add this entry to ~/.claude/kk-guard.json (substitute the absolute project path):

{"version":1,"projects":{"/absolute/path/to/repo":{"disable_selfmod":true}}}

This exception does not allow reading or writing secrets.

docs.title: Guard Configuration
docs.text:
The baseline ships inside the Claude plugin and runs even when neither configuration file exists. The standalone Codex guard plugin carries the same engine and declaration. These files are independent of provider permission settings:

File Owner and purpose <project>/.claude/kk-guard.json Committed project restrictions; adds secrets globs, destructive rules or protected paths ~/.claude/kk-guard.json Machine owner's exceptions; loosens destructive categories or self-modification protection for selected projects

docs.title: Project restrictions
docs.text:
Project configuration only adds protection. For example:

{
  "version": 1,
  "secrets": ["./**/local-secrets.json"],
  "selfmod": [".project-policy.json"],
  "destructive": {
    "deployment": [
      {"program": "deploy", "subcommand": "prod", "reason": "deploy prod changes production"}
    ]
  }
}

Secrets globs use ./**/ for project paths, ~/ for home paths, or // for absolute paths. They match requested and resolved paths. Project-relative policy stays anchored to the project root even when a shell runs in a subdirectory. Destructive rules use program, optional ordered subcommand, argument regex lists flags_any/flags_all/flags_none, and a reason; use the shipped declaration as the complete rule reference. The only supported named exemption is targets_under_tmp. Project config cannot disable categories or remove baseline rules. Template sync leaves this project-owned file alone.

docs.title: User exceptions
docs.text:
The user edits this file directly; the guard protects it from agent writes. Merge entries into an existing projects object rather than replacing other project entries. For example:

{
  "version": 1,
  "projects": {
    "*": {"allow_patterns": ["^git clean -n"]},
    "/absolute/path/to/ops": {"disable_categories": ["infra"]},
    "/absolute/path/to/agentstakk": {"disable_selfmod": true}
  }
}

Use physical absolute project paths (pwd -P). The engine combines * with the single longest matching directory prefix; shorter matching prefixes contribute nothing. Lists are combined, and disable_selfmod is enabled if either selected entry enables it. A parent path covers nested repositories and worktrees.

allow_patterns applies separately to each normalized simple command, including extracted shell bodies. Thus ^git clean -n can exempt git clean -nd, but not the rm in git clean -nd; rm -rf ./work. These patterns never exempt secrets or protected configuration. For sessions in the selected project, disable_selfmod permits edits to every path listed under Protected configuration, including the machine installation and plugin cache. The secrets policy still applies. On Codex, installed native forbids for rm, shred, sudo, su and doas still win over guard exceptions.

Missing config files leave the baseline active. Invalid JSON or invalid supported values produce a visible systemMessage and skip that file's changes; the other valid layer still applies. Unknown keys are reported and ignored. Secrets are never loosened by user configuration.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text:
The Claude plugin ships three hook handlers. It needs Bash, jq, Python 3.8+ and Claude Code 2.1.295+ for the declared onFailure: "block" behavior.

Hook Trigger Description Plugin root export SessionStart Exports TOOLBOX_PLUGIN_ROOT into the session environment so every Bash call has a reliable path to the plugin installation directory Session instructions SessionStart on startup, resume, clear and compaction Supplies the plugin’s behavioral instructions. Git-marketplace installs also supply plugin-root guidance. Each legacy project instruction file takes precedence over the corresponding hook text. Permission guard PreToolUse on Bash, Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit, and capy execution tools Enforces secrets, destructive-command rules, and protected configuration paths; denies on guard failures

Ordinary allowed calls produce no output and exit 0; invalid-config warnings may emit systemMessage. Denials emit JSON, a reason on stderr, and exit 2. Missing/broken interpreters, a corrupt declaration, crashes and malformed engine output deny the call. Claude also blocks hook failures/timeouts through onFailure: "block". A machine without a working Python interpreter blocks every matched tool, including reads, until repaired.

Codex adapters preserve the guard's denial reason and exit status. A normal policy denial does not mean the hook needs repair; the separate "adapter could not run" diagnostic indicates an adapter failure, such as a missing guard wrapper or unreadable hook input.

The wrapper runs the standard-library-only engine with -I -S, isolating Python environment/user-site settings and skipping unused site startup. On macOS it prefers Python at the standard Homebrew locations, then system Python; elsewhere it checks system Python first. PATH lookup remains the final fallback. Homebrew is not required.

Destructive operations are denied in every permission mode, including bypass mode. The reason names the matched category and the way through: the user runs the operation directly or configures an applicable exception. Disabling Claude hooks removes destructive and self-modification protection. Wrapped Claude sessions also carry the native secret denies. Bare Claude, the IDE extension and desktop sessions rely on the loaded plugin hook for the toolbox guard after migration.

The guard checks capy_execute, capy_execute_file, and capy_batch_execute even when capy is registered under a different MCP server name. Shell code uses the same checks as Bash; other languages use the literal-path, write-call and spawned-command scans described below. Every batch command is checked independently, and one denied command blocks the entire batch before execution.

For capy code, omitted cwd means the project root. Relative cwd overrides resolve from that root; absolute overrides select that directory. Each batch command starts in the selected directory. The capy_execute_file.path input stays project-root-relative regardless of where its processing code runs. These path parameters are literal paths, without shell-variable or tilde expansion.

Code in other languages, whether sent to capy or passed inline to an interpreter in Bash (python3 -c, node -e, a heredoc), is also checked for the commands it starts. The check is lexical. It runs when the code, with its line comments removed, names a process-starting call (subprocess, os.system, child_process, exec(, spawn, popen, exec.Command and similar) or contains a backtick string. Only the code counts here: a call that is merely named inside a string or a comment does not, except that a string which is exactly a spawn module's name ("child_process", "subprocess", "os/exec") is taken for an import. Every string literal is then read as a possible command and the destructive rules apply: a command string such as os.system("git reset --hard"), or adjacent literals forming an argument list such as ["kubectl", "-n", ns, "delete", "pod", name]. Category exceptions and allow_patterns apply as in Bash, where an exception matches a whole command: one that the code is still building, such as "rm -rf build " + extra, is matched with its unknown operand, as rm -rf build $extra would be. This is stricter than Bash in one respect: while a command is still being built, no exception applies to anything in it, including a complete command chained before the continuation or nested in a shell body, and a string passed through .split() counts as still being built. Code that names no such call keeps its literals as data. A literal that merely looks like a destructive command, in code that does name one, is denied.

The temporary-cleanup exemption is narrower here than in Bash. It applies only when the whole command is handed directly to a recognised spawn call, as a closed literal list or a single string, and every target is an absolute path under a temporary root: subprocess.run(["rm", "-rf", "/tmp/build"]). A command that is kept in a variable, concatenated, formatted or given a relative target does not earn it, because the guard cannot see what finally runs. Nor does one whose call takes further operands, as in exec.Command("rm", "-rf", "/tmp/build", extra). One known gap remains: a Node shell line followed by a variable argument list, spawnSync("rm -rf /tmp/build", args, {shell: true}), is treated as whole although Node appends args.

Deleting through a library call is treated as rm, whether or not the code starts a process. The recognised calls are Python's shutil.rmtree (also as rmtree imported by name), os.remove and os.unlink; Node's fs.rm, fs.rmdir and fs.unlink with their Sync forms, also when rmSync, rmdirSync or unlinkSync is imported by name; an unlink(...) function, whose target counts as unknown when it is given several; and an .unlink() method called without a positional argument, as on a pathlib path. A bare rm(...) or rmdir(...) is not one of them, and a call named in a comment or a string is ignored. The rm rule decides the rest, so the filesystem category, its exceptions and the temporary-cleanup exemption apply: shutil.rmtree("/tmp/build") is allowed, while a relative target or one that is not a single literal is denied, as rm "$dir" is in Bash.

This scan is a floor for ordinary code, not containment. It does not see a script that is written to a file and then run, a command assembled at runtime or across separate calls (cmd.append("delete"), a builder chain), a destructive library call other than those deletions (an API client, fs.promises, a deletion call in another language), or a spawn mechanism outside the recognized set. Code inside a string is scanned only where it is plainly run: after -c, -e or --eval in an argument list whose program is a known interpreter, or directly after a variable program such as sys.executable, not as the argument of exec(...) or eval(...). With a variable program, another option before the flag ([sys.executable, "-u", "-c", code]) hides the code, and the code is always read as interpreter code, so a shell body there ([shell, "-c", "rm -rf build"]) is not checked as a command. Inline code for php -r, Rscript -e and deno eval in Bash is not inspected at all.

Line comments are recognised without knowing the language: # or // at the start of a line or after whitespace begins one, and the rest of that line is not scanned for commands or deletion calls. Code that follows such a marker on the same line is therefore missed: after a Python floor division written a // b, after Lua's length operator in n = #items, or in a JavaScript private member declared at the start of a line. A marker attached to code, as in $#array, this.#field or a//b, is not a comment.

A command handed directly to a recognised spawn call as its first argument also gets the secrets and protected-configuration rules, as it would in Bash: subprocess.run("cat .env", shell=True) and subprocess.run(["cp", "payload", ".claude/settings.json"]) are denied. Every other literal gets the destructive rules only, so prose that mentions a secret path is not mistaken for a read. A command string that reaches the call through a variable is therefore checked for destructive commands but not for the secret paths inside it; a secret path that is a literal of its own is always checked.

Inspection is static: the guard does not execute submitted code or read the contents of an execute-file input. Paths assembled dynamically are outside its detection coverage, and non-shell mutation checks cover recognized literal write-call forms. Grep/Glob checks cover the search root, not every result's contents. Other execution tools need their own payload mapping. The Codex guard plugin supplies Bash, patch and capy adapters; see Codex limitations.

For shell paths, the guard retains possible directories after literal relative changes and checks existing matches of unquoted filename wildcards. Quoted or escaped wildcard characters remain literal. Interpreter checks decode common character escapes in literal paths while preserving raw strings. These checks inspect filenames and submitted text, without executing code or reading matched file contents.

docs.title: Project Instructions
docs.text:
To turn off the Claude plugin’s instruction hook, set claude.instructions to false in ${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-~/.config}/kk/config.json.

{"claude": {"instructions": false}}

The default is true. Plugin-only projects receive the toolbox’s behavioral guidance, including its task-tracking and commit-message conventions. The hook reads the switch at each matching session event. An invalid value fails the instruction hook with a diagnostic naming the configuration file. Claude still loads any instruction files that your project imports.

  • CLAUDE.md — project-specific instructions for Claude Code (checked into the repo)
  • .claude/CLAUDE.extra.md — legacy project instructions retained in some repositories. The machine plugin supplies behavioral instructions when the legacy file is absent.
  • AGENTS.md — equivalent instructions for Codex

docs.title: MCP Servers
docs.text:
MCP servers are configured at the user level (not in the repo) to keep API keys safe. These configs are generic enough to reuse across all your projects.

You don't need all servers to get started. Add them incrementally:

  1. Context7 (needs API key) — up-to-date library documentation and code examples
  2. Pal (API key optional) — multi-model AI integration for code review, debugging, planning, and security audit; without an API key, isolated reviews use your installed CLIs through clink
  3. Capy (optional, configured per project) — persistent knowledge base across sessions. Install with brew install serpro69/tap/capy.
Server Purpose Context7 Up-to-date library documentation and code examples Pal Multi-model AI integration — chat, debugging, code review, planning, security audit Capy Persistent knowledge base — cross-session project memory with FTS5 search

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
Note

Add MCP servers to ~/.claude.json under the mcpServers key.

Example mcpServers configuration 
{
  "context7": {
    "type": "http",
    "url": "https://mcp.context7.com/mcp",
    "headers": {
      "CONTEXT7_API_KEY": "YOUR_CONTEXT7_API_KEY"
    }
  },
  "pal": {
    "command": "sh",
    "args": [
      "-c",
      "$HOME/.local/bin/uvx --from git+https://github.com/serpro69/pal-mcp-server.git pal-mcp-server"
    ],
    "env": {
      "PATH": "/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:$HOME/.local/bin",
      "DEFAULT_MODEL": "auto",
      "DEFAULT_THINKING_MODE_THINKDEEP": "high",
      "GEMINI_API_KEY": "YOUR_GEMINI_API_KEY",
      "GOOGLE_ALLOWED_MODELS": "gemini-3.1-pro-preview,gemini-3-flash-preview"
    }
  }
}

See Pal configuration docs for model and thinking mode options.

Using claude-in-docker?

If you're using claude-in-docker images, replace npx and uvx calls with direct tool invocations. The images come with MCP tools pre-installed, avoiding dependency downloads on each launch:

"pal": {
  "command": "pal-mcp-server",
  "args": [],
  "env": { "..." }
}

Check your env settings, especially the PATH variable — custom paths not available in the image may cause the server to fail to connect.

docs.title: Codex
docs.text:
Note

MCP servers are added via codex mcp add and stored in ~/.codex/config.toml. Capy registers itself at the project level: run capy setup --platform codex in the project to add its MCP server to .codex/config.toml and its own Codex hooks to .codex/hooks.json. Capy’s hooks deliver guidance and HTTP routing. The machine guard covers supported capy execution calls. See Capy Hooks.

# Context7 — streamable HTTP, no API key env var needed (key is in the URL header)
codex mcp add context7 --url "https://mcp.context7.com/mcp"

# Pal — stdio server via uvx, with env vars for model config
codex mcp add pal \
  --env "PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:$HOME/.local/bin" \
  --env "DEFAULT_MODEL=auto" \
  --env "DEFAULT_THINKING_MODE_THINKDEEP=high" \
  --env "GEMINI_API_KEY=YOUR_GEMINI_API_KEY" \
  --env "GOOGLE_ALLOWED_MODELS=gemini-3.1-pro-preview,gemini-3-flash-preview" \
  -- sh -c "$HOME/.local/bin/uvx --from git+https://github.com/serpro69/pal-mcp-server.git pal-mcp-server"
Or manually add to ~/.codex/config.toml 
[mcp_servers.context7]
url = "https://mcp.context7.com/mcp"
http_headers = { "CONTEXT7_API_KEY" = "YOUR_CONTEXT7_API_KEY" }

[mcp_servers.pal]
command = "sh"
args = ["-c", "$HOME/.local/bin/uvx --from git+https://github.com/serpro69/pal-mcp-server.git pal-mcp-server"]
tool_timeout_sec = 1800 # increase timeout for clink-based reviews

[mcp_servers.pal.env]
DEFAULT_MODEL = "auto"
DEFAULT_THINKING_MODE_THINKDEEP = "high"
GEMINI_API_KEY = "YOUR_GEMINI_API_KEY"
GOOGLE_ALLOWED_MODELS = "gemini-3.1-pro-preview,gemini-3-flash-preview"
PATH = "/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin"

Verify with codex mcp list. See Pal configuration docs for model and thinking mode options.

docs.title: Context7
docs.text: Fetches current documentation for any library, framework, or SDK. Used by the /kk:dependency-handling skill to look up API signatures instead of guessing. Also available for ad-hoc queries.

docs.title: Pal
docs.text:
Multi-model AI integration. Powers the external reviewers of /kk:review-code:isolated and /kk:review-design:isolated — your change gets a second, independent review from an external model (another vendor's where the roster allows) in addition to the internal reviewer. Also provides: debug, planner, secaudit, testgen, and more.

The isolated review skills choose their external backend once per review from what Pal advertises (see Isolated reviews and external models):

  • API model configured (for example a Gemini key as above) → pal codereview.
  • No API model → pal clink, one review per installed CLI from a vendor other than the author's. Pal ships client manifests for claude, codex, agy and gemini; the plugin treats the first three as default providers and never uses gemini. This needs a Pal build whose listmodels returns CLI metadata in every mode: commit c73dab7d (2026-10-23) or a release containing it. The uvx --from git+… launch above installs current main.

Pal observes CLI executables at startup and caches its client registry: restart it after changing providers or client manifests.

CLI read access. Clink runs each CLI in your project root, but review criteria live in the plugin installation and the review bundle in the directory mktemp uses ($TMPDIR when set, otherwise /tmp; on macOS usually /var/folders/...). Denied reads are reported as lost coverage, never bypassed, so grant them once:

CLI Setup verified with the plugin Claude Code Use the machine launcher and a scoped read grant for temporary review files. See the client entry below. Antigravity (agy) Where its mode does not already permit reads, add "permissions": {"allow": ["read_file(/tmp)"]} (or your $TMPDIR, plus the plugin cache path) to ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/settings.json. No restart needed. Codex Shipped manifest worked unchanged in the verified setup; whether reads are sandboxed depends on your Codex configuration (not verified). Allow several minutes per CLI review and check tool_timeout_sec for long MCP calls.

docs.title: Claude client for machine installations
docs.text:
Copy PAL’s shipped conf/cli_clients/claude.json to ~/.pal/cli_clients/claude.json, or edit your existing override. PAL replaces the whole client definition. Keep the existing roles, model arguments and permission-mode arguments. Set these two fields in that definition. This Linux example also supports reviews initiated from a managed Codex installation with the default Codex home:

{
  "command": "kk claude",
  "additional_args": ["--allowedTools", "Read(//tmp/**)", "Read(~/.codex/plugins/cache/agentstakk-local/kk/**)"]
}

PAL splits command into the executable and its first argument. Put the directory containing kk on PAL’s PATH, or use the physical absolute path to the dispatcher followed by claude. Keep the real Claude CLI available on that path too. PAL starts a new process for each review, so wrapping your interactive session alone does not apply its settings to the reviewer.

The launcher’s default readRelease permission covers criteria loaded from the managed Claude release. Codex can pass criteria from its installed skills cache, so the example grants access to that plugin’s directory too. If CODEX_HOME is elsewhere, substitute its physical location. A Git-marketplace installation can have a different plugin directory: use the installed skill’s path to identify it. Scope the read to the skills plugin whose criteria the reviewer needs.

The temp grant covers the directory where the originating review creates its diff with mktemp. Substitute that directory’s physical absolute path for /tmp when needed. For example, for TMPDIR=/work/review-tmp the rule is Read(//work/review-tmp/**). On macOS check cd "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}" && pwd -P in the originating shell. Keep a dedicated review directory if other temporary files should stay outside this grant.

Restart PAL after editing the client. In a read-only clink review, check that the reviewer can read a criterion at the path supplied by the originating skill and the diff in the selected temporary directory.

Models stay configured where they are: Pal's model policy for API reviews, each CLI or client manifest for CLI reviews. To map a custom client name to its vendor, or to override the shipped defaults, declare it in the project's CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md (for example - \mycli` → Anthropic`).

docs.title: Capy (Knowledge Base)
docs.text:
Skills are knowledge-aware via Capy. They search for relevant context before executing (architecture decisions, review findings, language idioms) and index valuable learnings after producing output. Knowledge persists across sessions per-project using an FTS5 full-text search index.

Without Capy, each session starts fresh — all skills still work, they just don't carry learnings forward. Install when you want cross-session memory.

Installation: brew install serpro69/tap/capy then run capy setup in your project directory. Machine installation leaves capy registration to each project.

Codex: Run capy setup --platform codex to register its hooks and review them in /hooks. Wrapped sessions can also load .capy/AGENTS.md through a confirmed import in the root AGENTS.md. Capy hooks

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
The kk plugin ships per-domain profiles that make every workflow skill language-aware. Profiles provide:

  • Review checklists — language-specific code review items
  • Implementation gotchas — common pitfalls and idioms
  • Design prompts — architecture patterns relevant to the language
  • Test validators — testing conventions and frameworks
  • Documentation rubrics — what to document and how

docs.title: Supported Profiles
docs.text: Profile Covers Detection Go Go modules, packages, concurrency patterns *.go, go.mod, go.sum Java Maven/Gradle projects, Spring, JVM patterns *.java, pom.xml, build.gradle JS/TS Node.js, TypeScript, React, frontend tooling *.ts, *.tsx, *.js, package.json Kotlin Kotlin/JVM, Android, Gradle *.kt, *.kts, build.gradle.kts Kubernetes Helm charts, Kustomize, YAML manifests Chart.yaml, kustomization.yaml, K8s resource kinds K8s Operator kubebuilder, operator-sdk, controller-runtime PROJECT, config/crd/, controller-gen in Makefile Python Python implementation, testing, and review guidance *.py, *.pyi Skill MD Agent skill authoring (Claude Code, Codex) SKILL.md, files under a SKILL.md-rooted ancestor

docs.title: How Detection Works
docs.text:
Profiles activate automatically based on the files in your diff or working directory. Detection uses three signal types in cost order:

  1. Path signals — file extension globs (fast pre-filter, not authoritative alone)
  2. Filename signals — literal filenames like go.mod, Chart.yaml (authoritative)
  3. Content signals — anchors and patterns inside files (authoritative)

Multiple profiles can activate simultaneously — a Helm chart that generates Python scripts would trigger both k8s and python.

docs.title: What Profiles Provide
docs.text:
Each profile populates phase-specific content for the skills that consume it:

Phase Consuming Skill Content review-code/ /kk:review-code Language-specific review checklists, gotchas design/ /kk:design Architecture patterns, design considerations implement/ /kk:implement Implementation gotchas, idioms test/ /kk:test Testing frameworks, conventions, validators document/ /kk:document Documentation rubrics review-spec/ /kk:review-spec Spec conformance rules

docs.title: Python Implementation Guidance
docs.text:
For Python tasks, /kk:implement loads guidance on project compatibility, idioms, typing, exceptions, and resource ownership before editing. Async guidance is conditional on concrete async constructs or async-runtime imports in target files or planned edits; mentions in comments or strings do not trigger it.

The guidance applies to new .py files and .pyi stub changes as well as existing Python code. It follows the project's supported Python versions and existing tools. Packaging metadata alone does not activate the Python profile.

docs.title: Python Testing Guidance
docs.text:
For Python tasks, /kk:test loads behavioral testing guidance and a validator protocol before running checks. It follows the owning project's test command, environment, discovery settings, and configured quality gates. Pytest, unittest, and framework-specific entry points retain their existing role; the profile does not introduce a new toolchain.

Async testing guidance loads for concrete async code or explicit async-test configuration. Missing environments, unavailable tools, skipped async tests, and zero executed tests are reported as verification gaps. Stub changes use the project's available type/stub checks and relevant runtime tests.

docs.title: Vendored Content
docs.text: Some profiles vendor content from external upstream repositories. The Go profile, for example, vendors from samber/cc-skills-golang via a manifest-driven pipeline. See the Contributing Guide for details on the vendoring workflow.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text: The kk plugin ships 16 workflow and utility skills, including a complete development pipeline.

docs.title: The Pipeline
docs.text:
Use /kk:brainstorm when you want to think through a technical idea in conversation. It is optional: start with /kk:design whenever you want written planning.

/kk:design → /kk:review-design → /kk:implement → /kk:review-code → /kk:test → /kk:document
  1. /kk:design — turns an idea into design docs, an implementation plan, and a task list
  2. /kk:review-design — evaluates design docs for completeness and technical soundness
  3. /kk:implement — establishes behavior and constraints, executes tasks and hands current evidence to review
  4. /kk:review-code — reviews functional behavior, compatibility, SOLID, security and quality
  5. /kk:test — selects meaningful coverage, runs relevant checks and honors required repository/release suites
  6. /kk:document — updates architecture docs and records ADRs

docs.title: Skill Reference
docs.text: Skill What it does /kk:brainstorm Interviews anyone exploring a technical idea or decision, adapting depth to the next decision. Asks one question at a time and closes with decisions, rationale, and open assumptions in chat; creates no files. /kk:design Turns an idea into design docs, an implementation plan, and a task list in docs/feat/wip/. Asks refinement questions, then documents everything a developer needs to start coding. /kk:implement Executes a feature plan or standalone fix after establishing intended behavior, affected callers and delivery constraints. Refreshes evidence for independent review and distinguishes code completion from external release prerequisites. /kk:test Reuses or adds meaningful coverage, runs relevant checks and required repository/release suites, and reports actual results and limits. Chooses testing techniques to suit the requirement. /kk:document Updates project documentation and records ADRs for non-obvious decisions made during implementation. /kk:review-code Traces changed behavior and affected contracts, including unchanged callers and relevant historical sources, alongside SOLID/security/quality checks. Domain-specific guidance covers Go, Java, JS/TS, Kotlin, Python, Kubernetes, K8s Operator and agent skills. Standard and isolated modes. /kk:review-design Pre-implementation review gate. Evaluates design docs for completeness, internal consistency, and technical soundness before code is written. Standard and isolated modes. /kk:review-spec Compares implemented code against design/implementation docs. Finds spec deviations, missing implementations, and outdated docs — in both directions. /kk:model Produces or updates a domain-reference kit — a durable glossary + divergences/traps page pair per bounded context, with concept-to-code bindings. Its primary output is a decision queue of precise, role-tagged questions only a human can close. Runs upstream of /kk:design as the first producer of the architecture flow. /kk:review-architecture Reviews a written architecture artifact (ADR, architecture doc, a design doc's architecture section, or a domain-reference kit — glossary + traps pages reviewed as one composite artifact) against the system it describes. Claim-driven: extracts an inspectable claim-set, verifies mechanism existence/topology across seven dimensions, and grades decision soundness, reversibility, and provenance (self-certification of reverse-engineered claims). Security architecture is delegated to PAL secaudit. /kk:dependency-handling Fires before calling a library/SDK/API or adding a dependency. Forces a capy/context7 lookup instead of guessing signatures or behavior. /kk:diff-skill Compares two versions of a skill's markdown instructions to detect degradations and complexity increases. Asymmetric — only regressions count. /kk:merge-docs Merges two competing design docs for the same feature into one unified document, resolving conflicts and preserving the best of both. /kk:clarify-docs Improves selected documentation, PR drafts and issue descriptions after understanding requirements and source. Produces local edits, preserves meaning and respects the intended audience's access. /kk:handoff Explicitly publishes active-task context and a fresh-session starter prompt to a new secret GitHub gist. Uses existing GitHub CLI authentication; never initiates Capy indexing or archival. /kk:chain-of-verification Makes Claude fact-check its own answers. Standard mode (prompt-based) or isolated mode (independent sub-agents). For high-stakes accuracy.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Commands are skill variants invoked with explicit mode selection:

Command Invocation Description Code Review (isolated) /kk:review-code:isolated Functional, compatibility and quality review with independent reviewers CoVe (standard) /kk:chain-of-verification:default [question] Chain-of-Verification with prompt-based isolation CoVe (isolated) /kk:chain-of-verification:isolated [--explore] [--haiku] [question] CoVe with true sub-agent isolation Spec Review /kk:review-spec:default [feature] Verify code matches design/implementation docs Spec Review (isolated) /kk:review-spec:isolated [feature] Spec conformance review with independent sub-agent Template Sync /kk:template:sync [--version vX.Y.Z] [--dry-run] Sync repo with upstream template

docs.title: Functional review and implementation
docs.text:
Use /kk:review-code for an ordinary change review; functional reasoning is part of the existing invocation. The reviewer establishes the requested increment and review baseline, traces changed behavior through relevant unchanged callers, and checks meaningful success, boundary and failure scenarios. A specification helps, but the reviewer can use repository contracts and label inferred intent when formal design documents are absent.

For example, renaming a report label can be approved while an unchanged, disabled calculation has an inherited bug. Enabling that calculation by default is a different change: if valid empty input now crashes, the increment needs a fix. A feature flag only supports a compatibility claim when the affected paths actually obey it.

The report explains consequential findings, assessed paths and evidence limits. Compatibility can be Supported, Blocked, Unknown or Not applicable for the named baseline and scenarios. Missing deployment information does not automatically block a scoped code review; it does prevent certifying a deployment when that evidence is essential. Local tests and released-source inspection do not verify a live environment.

/kk:review-code:isolated prepares the relevant diff, current/historical source, task scope and review criteria for a named reviewer and PAL. If an external reviewer is unavailable or receives insufficient source, the report retains the available findings and discloses the lost coverage. Independent review does not guarantee correctness. See Isolated reviews and external models for how the external reviewers are chosen and what the report can claim.

/kk:implement applies the same behavioral context before editing, runs appropriate verification, and refreshes the evidence supplied to review. Use /kk:implement Fix the empty-note update while preserving omitted settings for a standalone change, or name a feature task to use its design and task records. A known unmet hard requirement keeps the task open. External activation work can remain separate when the agreed delivery contract permits it.

Testing focuses on agreed outcomes and consequential risks. Optional advice or minor report variation is not automatically a failure; an accurately explained inherited bug can be useful without prescribing its next action. Required checks still need actual execution. A denied compound command does not establish that every tool is unavailable: use an authorized direct route when appropriate, or report the specific unresolved check. Inspect that limit before treating a change as verified; the skills do not guarantee autonomous recovery in every session.

docs.title: Isolated reviews and external models
docs.text:
/kk:review-code:isolated and /kk:review-design:isolated run one internal sub-agent (code-reviewer or design-reviewer) plus external review through PAL. Standard mode never calls PAL.

Discovery-only selection. Once per review, before any external call, the skill checks PAL's tools and listmodels. With an eligible API model it runs the existing pal codereview flow. Without one, and with clink available, it runs one pal clink CLI review per eligible provider. If discovery fails or the PAL build does not expose CLI metadata, there is no external review and the report says so. The decision is frozen for that review: an API failure is reported as a failure and never switches to clink.

Roster. Candidates are PAL's configured CLI clients whose executable was found. The provider that authored the change (or, for design review, the documents) is excluded, one client per provider is attempted once, and a failed client is disclosed rather than retried or replaced. Provider identity is declared (in the request, the project's CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md, or client configuration you name), observed when a shipped client's configured or returned model shows another vendor, assumed from shipped manifest for PAL's shipped names (claude → Anthropic, codex → OpenAI, agy → Google; the report labels these and notes a declaration overrides them), or undeclared for any other name, which triggers one question before dispatch. gemini is retired and never a candidate. Cost scales with the roster: three shipped clients and a Claude-authored change give two CLI reviews.

Models and permissions stay yours. On the API branch the skill selects the most capable available model from PAL's catalog; on the clink branch it names no model, and each CLI review uses the model configured in the CLI or its PAL client manifest. Every request carries allow_edits=false and a no-edit prompt, which is a behavior contract, not an enforced sandbox; some CLIs keep their native permissions, and the report says so. CLIs must be able to read the plugin installation and the temp directory mktemp uses ($TMPDIR, otherwise /tmp), where criteria and evidence live; a denied read is reported as lost coverage, never bypassed. Per-CLI setup is in MCP Servers → Pal.

What the report claims. Each external reviewer is classified as requested, attempted, executed and adequately evidenced. Only observable read evidence counts as receipt; of the verified clients only Claude returns one, so codex and agy findings are kept with receipt unverified and cannot corroborate. A finding is corroborated only when two independent reviewers support it: an external reviewer counts only with observable receipt, the internal sub-agent counts through its source-tied report, and a corroboration resting on an assumed provider is labeled. Isolated design review is invoked as described in the /kk:review-design skill (/kk:review-design:isolated [feature] [scope]); it is a skill mode, not a separate command file. If every reviewer fails, the skill reports that isolated review did not complete and suggests standard mode instead of running it.

Minimum PAL. The clink path needs a PAL build whose listmodels returns cli_clients in every mode (commit c73dab7d, 2026-10-23, or a release that contains it). Restart PAL after changing provider or CLI configuration.

docs.title: Explore a technical idea
docs.text:
Use /kk:brainstorm Help me think through whether a local cache is worth adding to our developer tool to explore alternatives, challenge assumptions, and decide whether to pursue, discard, narrow, or investigate an idea. The audience includes developers, architects, and anyone considering technical products, infrastructure, tools, operations, or engineering workflows.

The interview asks one question at a time and adapts its depth to your next decision. It reads relevant project files or web sources when evidence could change the advice, so a repository is optional. When a premise changes, it revisits affected decisions while preserving unrelated ones. Missing evidence stays explicit.

The result is a chat recap of settled decisions and their rationale, open assumptions, details that can wait, and the next decision or investigation. If you stop early, it recaps the partial discussion without claiming the idea is validated. The skill creates no files or saved interview state and performs no knowledge-store or session-vault searches, indexing, or implementation.

When written planning would help, the skill may suggest /kk:design. You choose whether to invoke it; the recap supplies context for its existing confirmations. Brainstorming does not invoke another workflow automatically and is not required before design. For a durable domain glossary and traps pages, use /kk:model; for a build or fix, use /kk:implement. Nontechnical brainstorming is outside this skill's scope.

docs.title: Continue in a fresh session
docs.text:
Invoke /kk:handoff in Claude Code or $kk:handoff in Codex when you want to restart a conversation or move to another provider or machine. Invocation requests publication to GitHub, using an already installed and authenticated gh CLI. Both hosts disable implicit selection: an ordinary summary or request to refresh review context does not invoke this skill.

Each invocation creates a new secret gist containing handoff.md (active-task intent, decisions, progress, evidence limits and next action) and prompt.md (a short starter prompt containing the real gist URL). Secret means unlisted: anyone with the link can read it. The agent checks outgoing content and removes credentials and unrelated private information before upload. This instruction-based check does not guarantee comprehensive detection; a secret gist is not access-controlled private storage.

The agent returns the URL and ready-to-paste prompt when both gh writes succeed, without inspecting the published gist afterward. Paste the prompt into the destination session to explicitly load the named handoff, reconcile the current project state and continue. No resume skill or automatic discovery is involved. Uncommitted changes stay on the source machine: the gist does not transfer your worktree, credentials or Capy database.

Existing Capy sources or archived sessions may be referenced only when prior indexing or archival of the relevant material is already evidenced. These references remain optional; the handoff never initiates indexing, fetch-and-index or archival, directly or through another tool, skill, agent or the starter prompt. The summary remains useful if the destination cannot open those references.

Preparation uses a unique temporary directory outside the repository. After success, the agent removes those files where host policy permits; gists remain until you delete them. Publication failure or uncertainty preserves local recovery content and reports its absolute paths and any known partial gist URL, without automatic retries or remote inspection. A local cleanup failure is reported separately from successful publication. The skill does not install/authenticate gh or switch storage when access is unavailable.

docs.title: Other utilities
docs.text:
/kk:dependency-handling is pulled in automatically during implementation whenever you touch an external library, SDK, or API — it routes through capy/context7 instead of guessing.

/kk:review-spec verifies code matches design/spec and detects deviations — use during or after implementation.

/kk:model produces the domain-reference kit (glossary + traps pages) and a role-tagged decision queue for a bounded context — use before feature design when the domain's concepts, code bindings, or open questions need mapping.

/kk:review-architecture reviews an ADR, architecture doc, or domain-reference kit against the codebase it claims to describe — use after an architecture artifact is written, before or during implementation.

/kk:merge-docs reconciles competing design docs into one unified document.

/kk:chain-of-verification adds self-verification for high-stakes accuracy at any stage.

docs.title: Clarify an existing document
docs.text:
Use /kk:clarify-docs docs/configuration.md for service owners; use src/config/ to improve an existing guide, or select a design document or implementation plan for the developer who needs to resume the work. Supply the target paths and any known audience, purpose, requirements or source references. A directory helps find the target; it does not authorize rewriting every document inside it.

The skill first understands the requirements and relevant implementation, then edits the selected document in place. It explains purpose and behavior before reference detail while preserving requirements, exceptions, decisions, task state and links. Source disagreements and missing context remain explicit with a next step. No additional summary file is produced, and a document that already meets the requirements stays unchanged. Clear prose can still receive a source-backed factual correction.

This utility improves existing documentation, PR drafts and issue descriptions, saving results locally. It does not change code or configuration, publish externally, or edit agent/skill instructions. An explicit AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md or SKILL.md target receives a suggestion to use /kk:implement, with no edit or invocation of implementation. Generic requests for shorter chat answers do not activate it.

The final comprehension and fidelity check runs in the editing session. Normal project review remains the caller's responsibility; the skill does not provide independent runtime verification or a guarantee of improved human comprehension.

docs.title: Optional clarification after drafting
docs.text:
/kk:design and /kk:document suggest /kk:clarify-docs after creating or materially revising documents, naming the relevant paths. You decide whether to run it. Neither writing skill loads the clarification procedure or applies a separate editorial pass automatically. Both remain responsible for clear, accurate drafts and their required content.

Entry point Recommendation and review boundary /kk:design for a fresh idea Suggests clarification of all created design, implementation and task documents, including split parts, before recommending /kk:review-design. Neither follow-up runs automatically. /kk:design resuming WIP Suggests clarification of only materially refined documents before recommending review and handing off. An unchanged resume does not rewrite documents or suggest clarification. /kk:document Suggests clarification of created or materially revised outputs; no suggestion when there are none. Project-prescribed review remains separate. /kk:implement plan mode Calls /kk:document when the whole plan completes, which may suggest clarification. It runs no automatic clarification pass; individual tasks do not trigger this completion call. /kk:implement standalone mode No automatic documentation completion call. Invoke /kk:document to update documentation or /kk:clarify-docs to edit existing prose explicitly.

For example, /kk:design refining only implementation.md suggests clarification of that path, leaving the linked design outside the suggested edit scope. Clarification improves the explanation; /kk:review-design evaluates the design. If you choose both, clarify first so the review assesses the final wording. The standalone clarification skill's fidelity check remains in-session, not independent verification.

docs.title: Clarify a PR draft
docs.text:
Use /kk:clarify-docs pr-draft.md for repository reviewers to edit a local draft in place. Supply the PR or base/head context and any relevant requirements. The skill checks the actual review diff and source before explaining what this increment delivers, which files deserve attention and what validation supports it. A contract change is described separately from future runtime integration. The draft identifies newly added tests and records validation outcomes and limits; those details belong in the draft, even when the completion message reports them.

Use /kk:clarify-docs <PR URL>; save to docs/feat/wip/import/pr-draft.md to obtain a PR body through read-only tools and produce a local draft. Pasted bodies work the same way. Without a supplied destination, the skill names a draft under the clearly established current feature directory; if neither is clear, it asks before writing. Unrelated existing files are never overwritten. Missing source access stays explicit and limits what the draft claims. No PR update, comment or message is sent by this workflow.

Declare the intended audience and any private sources. Explicit restrictions take precedence even for tracked files. Otherwise, files tracked at the PR head can be referenced for that repository's review audience, including shared task documents. External references need evidence that the audience can access them; the editor's credentials alone are insufficient. Private context may help explain the work, but removing its citation does not make its facts shareable. The skill uses an accessible source or an explicitly authorized explanation, or retains a limitation.

Destination drafts, shared reports and gap notes exclude absolute workspace paths and private source pointers. A completion message visible only to you may use an absolute link to the selected local output so you can open it. That exception does not authorize sharing private source paths or facts.

docs.title: Clarify an issue description
docs.text:
Use /kk:clarify-docs to explain an existing bug report, feature request or other issue for its intended readers. Select the description and any known audience, requirements or source references:

  • Local draft: /kk:clarify-docs issue-draft.md; preserve the reported reproduction details.
  • Issue URL: /kk:clarify-docs <GitHub or Linear issue URL>; save to docs/feat/wip/import/issue-draft.md.
  • Pasted description: /kk:clarify-docs the issue description pasted below; save to drafts/import-issue.md, followed by the body.

The selected local draft is edited in place. Remote and pasted bodies become one local draft at your destination, or an unused path within a clearly established feature directory. Without either, the skill inspects available context and asks where to save before writing. A captured body is input, not permission to overwrite that file; unrelated existing drafts are protected. GitHub and Linear are examples: the skill uses available read-only tools or supplied text and requires no particular tracker integration. It sends no issue updates, comments or messages.

Bug reports retain reproduction steps, commands, environment/version details and expected versus observed results. Reported behavior stays distinct from verified behavior, including differences between the reported version and inspected source. Feature requests preserve accepted intent, proposals, existing acceptance criteria and open decisions. Future implementation and a PR diff are not prerequisites. Missing decisions or criteria remain unknown with a next step and a known or explicitly unknown owner where relevant. The skill neither invents criteria nor executes reproduction commands. Tracker titles and types are read-only context; supplied titles stay unchanged, with no replacement-title suggestions.

If the body is inaccessible, the skill requests its text or an accessible source without writing a purported revision. If only supporting evidence is unavailable, it can still clarify the supplied body while preserving verification limits. Conflicting requirements and source remain explicit with a next action.

For a GitHub issue in repository R, the default readers are R's issue audience unless you specify another audience. Files tracked in R at the inspected revision are presumed accessible to those readers, including in a private repository; the default branch supplies the revision when none is established. This does not verify behavior in an older reported version. Explicit restrictions override that presumption, even for tracked files. Another audience, repository or tracker needs evidence of sharing; a Linear link or the editor's credentials alone does not prove access. Restricted facts and pointers stay out of both the draft and shared report, including uncited paraphrases. The caller-only output-link exception described above applies only to the selected local draft.

Requests to implement, fix or work on an issue use /kk:implement; an issue URL alone does not request description editing. Clarification remains a separate, optional action after drafting, with the same in-session fidelity check and normal project review described above.

docs.title: Migrate a template repository
docs.text: kk migrate retires the legacy toolbox files in one Git repository. Installing or upgrading kk on a machine leaves those files in place. Run the migration once per repository, after the people who rely on its protections have installed and verified the machine release. The result is an ordinary, uncommitted Git diff.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
1. Check for .github/template-state.json at the repository root. Review local changes with git status. Copy out edits to synced files that you want to keep, or add their paths to the manifest’s sync_exclusions.
  2. Install kk. For Codex, open plain codex in this repository without a named profile, review folder trust and all three managed guard hooks in /hooks, then exit. Run kk status --live to check the installed guards. Migration also reads the effective guard configuration in this repository for each tool it uses. A scratch workspace prevents a legacy hook from supplying a misleading denial.
  3. Close Codex sessions opened before kk was installed and its hooks reviewed. An older session may lose protection when its legacy scripts disappear. Sessions opened after the machine guard is ready can keep using it. The legacy sync script needs Bash 4 or newer (including on macOS). Put that bash, curl and Mike Farah’s yq on PATH for migration.

docs.title: Preview, sync and retire
docs.text:
From the repository, run:

kk migrate

A manifest naming serpro69/claude-toolbox or serpro69/claude-starter-kit can migrate with the renamed upstream. A fork’s manifest must match the repository that supplied the migration scripts. Sync exclusions still apply. If Git maps a former upstream to a different mirror, align its insteadOf rule with the current upstream before retrying migration.

The default retirement tag is v0.26.0-rc.4, the last full template. The sync script, its version helper and the template it renders all come from that tag. If you are still running the RC4 or earlier pilot CLI, use kk migrate --retirement-version v0.26.0-rc.4 explicitly. The same option can select a future retirement maintenance tag.

  1. Sync to the retirement release. Read the preview before confirming. Like any sync, this step overwrites edits to synced files. Migration preserves adopter-owned settings and hooks during the merge, including custom deny entries. Files under sync_exclusions stay untouched. An up-to-date repository skips the sync confirmation.
  2. Retire the legacy files. The second preview compares the repository with that same tag’s rendered template. It lists matching files and toolbox entries to remove, custom or excluded files to keep, and the effect on collaborators. Decline this step to leave the repository synced with its legacy guard in place. Rerunning kk migrate previews the remaining work.

Inspect git diff and git status before committing. You can keep individual changes out of the migration commit, for example the project rules file or a plugin registration used by CI. Preserve the files or marketplace definitions that a retained registration needs.

Migration keeps the legacy scripts together when you exclude .codex/hooks.json or a retained handler names the .codex/scripts directory. If your hook delegates to a separate program that depends on those scripts, exclude the script directory explicitly. Excluding an absent provider directory keeps it absent during migration sync.

docs.title: What changes for the team
docs.text: Repository change Effect after the commit Legacy Codex guard registrations, scripts and native forbids are removed Each machine needs a reviewed guard plugin. Native forbids return on machines that enable the account-wide rules file. Committed plugin enablement and Git-marketplace registration are removed Cloud sessions, fresh CI runners and collaborators without a machine install may lose the plugin. Provision those hosts or retain the relevant project configuration. Template Claude deny entries and statusline are removed kk claude supplies the native denies and statusline. Bare Claude, IDE and desktop sessions rely on loaded plugin hooks for the toolbox guard. Project choices survive The report lists adopter deny entries, hooks, non-default manifest choices, and the Codex sandbox_mode, approval_policy and approvals_reviewer settings. These three lines continue to take precedence in the project. Delete them yourself to hand those decisions to each machine. Toolbox instruction imports and sync infrastructure are retired An import whose customised or excluded target remains is kept. Add an @path line to the root AGENTS.md for each repository file you want kk codex to inject. Codex instructions

docs.title: Ordinary sync and the retirement boundary
docs.text:
Ordinary local and CI syncs to the retirement release still update the legacy template and print migration guidance. Removal requires the separate retirement operation. A repository using a sync script older than v0.21.0 must not sync past the retirement release. Use the retirement release as the latest possible sync target until migration. From v0.21.0 onwards, the local script hands control to the target version’s script before applying project changes.

Use --version v0.26.0-rc.4 locally or enter v0.26.0-rc.4 in the workflow’s version field to sync to the last full template. If an older local updater reports a missing semver-compare.sh, run kk migrate for retirement. To continue ordinary sync, restore the helper from the same tag as the installed updater before retrying.

The default branch and releases after RC4 carry a small compatibility script at the old sync path. A supported old client hands control to it. It prints migration guidance, exits successfully and reports has_changes=false to CI, so the workflow opens no sync PR. Some clients can backfill their own manifest before handing over.

For maintenance of a repository still using the old updater, the versioned reference covers sync exclusions, GitHub Actions credentials and settings merges. Legacy template-sync reference at v0.25.4

A running session is supported for 14 days after its machine release is superseded. Restart older sessions within that window. Use kk rollback to restore a retained machine release. Repository migration changes have their own history in Git.
